maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday the Prime Minister in announcing that an acreage payment would be made to western grain producers outlined the reasons why the government felt that action of this sort was necessary and why this particular form of payment has been decided upon. I shall attempt in my remarks not to cover again the ground which the Prime Minister covered so adequately yesterday.


During the past three years a very large number of schemes and proposals for assistance to western grain producers have been made by the western members of parliament, by farm organizations, by individual farmers, and so on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: By the opposition in particular.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I have not heard any from the opposition, actually, which had not first been proposed by somebody else. I think the opposition has been notably deficient in any original thinking with regard to this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You are deficient in mind and thinking.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition says "deficient in mind and thinking", and I agree with him; I think they have been notably deficient in any kind of thinking, particularly in any original thinking. However, Mr. Chairman, after careful consideration of a very large number of these different schemes and proposals, the government has come to the conclusion that an acreage payment as proposed in this estimate is the fairest way to extend assistance at the present time. The difficulty, of course, is to provide that assistance in such a way that you do not create further serious problems by the very fact that the assistance is being provided. If support for any particular commodity is given in a way which provides an incentive to the production of that commodity, you inevitably have a pile-up of surpluses which in present world conditions are extremely difficult to dispose of, and you probably create problems which are just as serious in their way as the problem you are attempting to solve.
I remember reading an editorial not long ago, I think it was in the Christian Science Monitor, in which a sort of philosophical discussion was going forward as to ways in which government could assist various sectors of the economy. The editorialist stated something which I think to be true, although most people do not realize it. He said that most of the problems faced by government could be solved if you were able to raise sufficient money in taxes and apply that money to the alleviation of the situation you find. Whether it is a matter of a defence program, old age assistance, hospitalization or any of those things, if you put enough money into it, provided you can raise enough money by taxation, you can cure a particular problem. Then he went on to say that agriculture is entirely different from this point of view; agriculture is a field into which the more money you pour the more problems you create for yourself.

The man writing the article made reference to the wheat situation in the United States, where enormous sums of money ranging into the billions have been spent to support the price of wheat. The result has been a very great expansion of the wheat area of the United States. Whereas most of the wheat used to be grown in the areas climatically best suited to its production, the middle west and so on, now wheat is being grown in every state of the union and, in addition, is being produced in greatly increased quantities. Thus the amount of money which has been poured into that commodity in the United States has produced greater problems than those that existed before all this money was spent.
In providing assistance, this is one of the things you always have to keep in mind and it is one of the great problems which have to be solved; the assistance must be provided in such a way that it will not stimulate production and thus create a surplus and give rise to fresh problems.
When this sort of thing happens you also get difficulties from the strictly agricultural point of view. The economic utilization of soil resources is interfered with, and you get a general imbalance in the agricultural economy.
On that general point I think one could say that two of the essentials of any form of agricultural assistance which may be provided are, first, this matter I have been talking about, that the assistance should not serve as an incentive to pile up unsaleable surpluses; second, that the type of assistance should not be such as to serve as an impediment to the marketing or free trade of the commodity which you are supporting. The acreage payment we are proposing meets both these basic requirements.
The so-called deficiency payments which so many hon. members opposite said we should have paid, and which were requested by western farmers do not, on the other hand, meet these two basic requirements. If these deficiency payments had been made there is no question but that they would have stimulated a very great increase in the amount of wheat production. The acreage of wheat in Canada at the present time is some six or seven million acres less than it was some ten years ago, but if the scheme proposed, which was really a disguised form of the same type of price support for wheat which has been in effect in the United States for many years, had been put into effect here the inevitable result would have been the same as in the United States; that is, to cause a great deal more land to be put into wheat production, a great increase in the amount
Supply-Agriculture
of wheat produced and consequently an intensification of the serious surplus situation for wheat not only in Canada but in the world as a whole. Therefore it would have been unsound from that point of view.
In addition to that, of course, an increase in wheat production would have meant that once more the beneficial diversification of agriculture which has taken place in western Canada would have gone backward. Many people who have gone into other types of production would have dropped that and gone back into wheat because straight wheat farming involves much less work. It is an easier type of agriculture than raising livestock, where daily attention and care are required.
Well, from the other point of view, the availability of foreign markets, there is no question about it, as the Leader of the Opposition at least knows very well, that most countries in the world are not prepared to accept subsidized exports. There are very few places in which you can sell commodities at a subsidized price in competition with the commodities of the country to which you wish to export and in competition with other countries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman, not to make it difficult for the minister to proceed but so that we may have a little clarification. The item before the committee is a specific item, and we are now having from the Minister of Agriculture what we had from the Prime Minister yesterday, a discussion of the overall policy of the government on agriculture. Personally I do not object, but this is out of order. If we are to have a wide debate on agriculture it should be clearly understood that that will be a privilege accorded not only to members of the ministry but to us as well in the opposition who sometimes find, not because of you, Mr. Chairman, but because of obstruction from hon. gentlemen opposite, great difficulty in extending our remarks beyond the particular item.
Therefore it must be clearly understood now that this general discussion on which the Minister of Agriculture is launching is a general discussion that must not be denied to other hon. members; otherwise the Chair must take the position that all we can discuss is the particular item before the committee. I know the hon. member for Greenwood, who looks so intent, fully agrees with me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I maintain that the contention the hon. member has

Supply-Agriculture
made is completely incorrect. Everything I have said has been directed to this particular item. I am not going into a general discussion of agriculture; I am talking about assistance which is being provided to western farmers by this estimate. I am explaining why this particular type of assistance, in the opinion of the government, is much preferable to the type of assistance the western farm organizations and some members of the opposition asked us to put into effect, namely the so-called deficiency payments on western wheat, oats and barley. Everything I have said is directly related to the estimate under consideration, and in no way is a general discussion of agricultural matters. If I were on a general discussion of agricultural matters I would certainly discuss a lot of other things completely unrelated to this particular point.
That is what I have to say with regard to the point of order. It seems to me the hon. member is either attempting to interfere with my remarks by raising this particular point of order, or otherwise trying to lay the groundwork for a general speech he himself has prepared on agriculture. I would think the latter is the more likely reason for his interruption. I see the hon. member for Essex East smiles and applauds that comment. I agree with the hon. member's point of order, that this should not be a general discussion of agriculture, but certainly all the remarks I have made have been related directly to the item under discussion.
I have been emphasizing particularly the point that any form of assistance provided should meet two essential requirements; that it does not serve as an incentive to produce unsaleable surpluses, and that it is not of the type which interferes with our marketing of the product either in home or export markets. I have made the point that the so-called deficiency payments asked for would not meet either of these tests. With respect to the latter, may I point out the fact that most countries in the world will not accept subsidized exports. All the signatories to GATT object to them. Therefore if so-called deficiency payments had been put into effect on western wheat, oats and barley it would have been much more difficult for us to market these products abroad. We have to market most of our wheat abroad, and in some places where we are selling wheat at the present time, it might not have been possible to sell it at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You should not have promised it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
These are the two outstanding and compelling reasons why the request for so-called deficiency payments could

not be acceded to. On the other hand, the acreage payment has neither of these disadvantages, and it meets the two basic requirements for a type of assistance which will not get us into a lot more serious trouble.
In addition, the acreage payments which are proposed here meet another very important requirement, in that they extend proportionately the greatest aid to the farmers who need that aid the most. They extend the greatest aid to the small farmers, those farmers who have had poor crops or have lost their crops because of adverse climatic conditions, hail, drought, flooding or whatever it may be. Deficiency payments would extend no aid to these people, because if they were not able to grow a crop on account of adverse conditions they would not get any deficiency payment. Therefore, under the deficiency payment plan the people who need help the most would get no help whatever. Small farmers, who need aid far more than the larger farmers, would only get a very small proportion of the assistance.
The Prime Minister pointed out on March 4, as found on page 1769 of Hansard, that under the so-called deficiency payment proposal 35 per cent of the western farmers, the smaller farmers, would receive only 14 per cent of the payments, and that the other 65 per cent covering the larger farmers having 200 cultivated acres or more would receive 86 per cent of the money provided. Surely that is not a reasonable sort of proposition or the form in which aid should be extended. Surely it should be extended to the people who need aid the most, and not primarily to those people who are in the best financial position and therefore need it the least.
As I said a little earlier, acreage payments do give the same amount of assistance to most of the smaller farmers as to the larger farmers, and they also provide assistance to the people who have had poor crops or who have lost their crops for any reason whatever. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I should like to place on the record a breakdown of the permit holders in western Canada for the 1959-60 crop year. It is in the form of a table and I wish to comment on it, but first I would ask the permission of the committee to have the table printed in Hansard.

If you add together those first three groups you find they total 124,669. The total number of permit holders is 224,717. So we find that approximately 125,000 out of approximately
225,000	permit holders have a cultivated acreage of 248 acres or less. In other words they have considerably less than a half section
of land under cultivation. This is contrary to the idea that many people particularly, in eastern Canada, have, that the western farmers are all big farmers; that they have thousands of acres of land; that they go to California in the wintertime, and things along that line. These are all myths which have been perhaps, we will say, made the subject of jokes. As a result a lot of people, because these things have been repeated over and over, have come to believe them. But these figures show the fact, that 125,000 out of
225.000	farmers in western Canada have a cultivated acreage, as I say, of 248 acres or less or less than half a section.
These 125,000 farmers out of the 225,000 will receive slightly more than half the total assistance provided, more than half of the $41 million to $42 million which will be provided in this way. In other words the smaller farmers, who constitute the bulk of the farmers, will receive more than half of the assistance provided. This makes a very, very much fairer way of providing assistance than one based on the number of bushels that a man produces, which is what was asked for.

Yes. I wanted to have this table put on the record because I think it is very interesting and very illuminating. It particularly demonstrates this point I have just been making, that the great majority of farmers in western Canada are not big farmers; they are small farmers, 125,000 out of 225,000. They are the people who particularly need assistance, and they are the people to whom this scheme provides the bulk of the assistance.
The producers of western wheat, oats and barley, as hon. members of the house know, are the only people who are not provided benefits under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Every other agricultural product in Canada is eligible for support under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. During the past two years we have supported some 20-odd commodities under that act. As a result of that, as a result of some increased tariff protection which we have provided, and as a result of import quotas and restrictions,	particularly on dairy
products, producers of agricultural products other than western wheat, oats and barley on the whole have received prices as good as or better than have been received by farmers in any other country in the world.
I would just like to demonstrate that by a few figures, to show what the returns for farmers engaged in other branches of agriculture have been in Canada during the past two years, as compared with farmers in other countries. This will show that the support we have provided under the Agricultural Stabilization Act by import controls and some tariff protection has meant that farmers other than the western wheat, oats and barley producers have received a large measure of support and have enjoyed prices which have compared very, very favourably with those of farmers in any other country.
If we take the case of cattle, in 1959 good steers in Toronto averaged $25.10; in Australia, $11.12, less than half as much; in Denmark, $13.96; in New Zealand, $7.60; in the United Kingdom, $19.09, and in the United States, $25.48, practically the same as in Canada. We were $25.10 and they were $25.48. That is the picture on cattle. In the Antipodes the price was well under a half, in one case a third, of what our farmers were getting for cattle in 1958.
In 1958 the picture is much the same. If we take the case of hogs in 1958, in Canada the figure was $29.13; in Australia, $25.75; in Denmark, $25.75; the United Kingdom, $25.79, and the United States $27.02. Our price was higher than any of those countries. The only country which was as high or higher than ours was West Germany.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, once more I must point out that I am relating this directly to the situation of the western farmers. I am pointing out that farmers, apart from the producers of western wheat, oats and barley, have enjoyed the advantages of the Agricultural Stabilization Act and of various other support measures which have been provided by this government. As a result they have enjoyed prices much better than many other countries and as good as any in any country of the world.

Let us take lambs as an example. The prices in 1959 were as follows: Canada, $21.15; Australia, $8.24; New Zealand, $8.59; the United Kingdom, $13.41; the United States, $20.64. The highest price for lambs in any of those countries was that paid in Canada.
If you take dairy products you find the same thing. The price paid here was the highest in any country in the world except in West Germany, where the price was slightly above ours. Butter prices in 1959 were as follows:	Canada, 63.2 cents;
Australia, 47 cents; Denmark, 41 cents; West Germany, 66 cents; New Zealand, 33 cents; New Zealand butter selling in the United Kingdom, 41 cents; the United States, 58 cents.

The same thing applies to cheese. The 1959 prices were as follows: Canada, 37.1 cents; Australia, 28 cents; Denmark, 23 cents; West Germany, 33 cents; New Zealand, 20 cents; Canadian cheese selling in the United Kingdom, 41 cents, New Zealand at 35 cents and Dutch at 33 cents; United States Cheddar cheese, 31 cents. This compares with a price of 37 cents in Canada.
The hon. member mentioned eggs a little while ago. The average price for grade A large eggs in 1959 was 43.1 cents a dozen in Canada and 32 cents in the United States, a difference of 11 cents in our favour. Prices in other countries were as follows: Denmark, 31 cents; West Germany, 42 cents; British domestic eggs in Great Britain, 48 cents. That was the highest price for eggs any place.
I could deal with potato prices and the prices of other products, but I will not take any more time in dealing with this subject. What these figures	demonstrateand this is the point I want to make -is that agriculture in this country has received a large measure of protection through the stabilization act. As a result the farmers of this country have received very good prices compared with those received in any other country in the world you wish to take, and very much higher prices than in most of those countries.
The wheat farmer and the western oats and barley grower have not had the advantage of this stabilization act; therefore some special type of assistance is required in order to balance things off. This is one of the things which is necessary in providing assistance to agriculture, that you balance the kind of assistance you give to different commodities and to different regions or areas and so forth. You have to keep the assistance in balance; otherwise you get a surplus production in one line and a reduction in production in the other, you have a shortage of one commodity and a surplus of another. I mention this in order to show that the payment of this particular form of assistance to western farmers is necessary, required and desirable in every way, in my opinion.

I thank the committee for extending my time and wish to assure them than I will not speak at undue length.
As the Prime Minister pointed out yesterday, the western farmer has been aware that he was not under the stabilization act as far as wheat, oats and barley were concerned. Western farmers and farm organizations, and particularly western members of the Conservative party, have been pushing for many years, really, for the introduction of what is generally referred to as a two-price system for wheat. This payment will give to western farmers the equivalent of a two-price system for wheat. It will give them a sum such as they would receive if the proportion of their wheat used for human consumption in Canada were placed under a two-price system at a very considerably increased price over the general world market price.
One other point I should like to make is that the money provided by this vote will have an extremely beneficial effect on the whole Canadian economy. The farmers who receive this money are not going to put it in a sock and keep it there. This money will be going into circulation and will roll through the whole economy. It will mean that sales of all kinds will be stimulated. The result will be a considerable increase in employment, in manufacturing, merchandising, transportation and so on. From that point of view the benefits of the payment will be spread all throughout Canada.

The demand was for deficiency payments for the 1955-56, 1956-57 and 1957-58 crops. It was only for the latter of those three years that this government was in power. In other words, the farmers asked for a payment to make up for the losses they maintained they had suffered under the government of which the hon. member for Essex East was a distinguished member.

What sparked this demand for deficiency payments on the part of western farmers was the fact that the previous government gave them very little support of any kind. During that period they suffered a considerable decrease in income, and their grain was not being sold. It was being sold in constantly decreasing amounts until we came into power and stepped up the sales of western wheat in particular.
This fact is clearly shown by the net income per farm worker during those periods. In 1953, which was one of the big years, the net income per farm worker was $2,740 but in 1954 it was only $1,367, less than half as much. This is what started a great deal of the agitation in western Canada for assistance of this kind. In 1955 it was $2,071. In 1956 there was a good crop and a fair sale and it rose to $2,783, but then in 1957 it was down again to $1,617. In 1958 it was back up to $2,170 and in 1959 it was $2,410.
The hon. member for Essex East said that net farm income in 1959 was less than in 1958. I have given the net income per farm worker. The net income per farm, of course, was greater than that. I mentioned those figures to show that although the net income for all farmers in 1959 was somewhat less than in 1958, nevertheless the net income per farm worker was more in 1959 than in 1958. The statement which the hon. member for Essex East also made in speaking yesterday, along the line that the net income in 1959 was below that of 1958, is one which he is very fond of making. He never relates it to the fact that the net income in 1958 was 28 per cent higher than in 1957.

The farmers sold wheat to Great Britain at below world prices because of the deal which the government of which the hon. member was a member cooked up. They thought the farmers of western Canada were going to become too wealthy, and so they curtailed their income.

Canadian farmers are getting three times the subsidy help from the taxpayer they were getting as recently as five years ago.
So at least somebody realized it; somebody realized that this government is giving some substantial help to the farmers. I am certain the farmers in my constituency will appreciate it to quite an extent.
The hon. member for Vancouver East, when he spoke about this in the house yesterday, seemed a bit worried about the small farmer who had less than 200 acres. What would happen to the small farmer under the deficiency payment program that his party advocated? I do not know what the Liberal party has advocated, because they have never yet said in this house what they do advocate.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
The only thing I can do is judge them by experience. Then that would be nothing, because they have done nothing. The hon. member for Vancouver East seemed worried about the small farmer. What would happen, under the deficiency payment idea to the farmer who was hailed out or dried out in the past year or this year, or had his crops snowed under last year and because of late harvesting last fall it was frozen and damp and he decided to feed it to cattle during the winter? What would happen to him under the deficiency payment idea? He would get nothing at all. There were a great many farmers in western Canada who did harvest their crops as late as November and part of December last year and, finding their grain a bit damp and too hard to move, fed it to cattle and hogs.

Supply-Agriculture
So the hon. member tor Vancouver East seems a bit worried about the small farmer. Under this type of program the small farmer is getting something. Under the other it is questionable whether he would have got anything. Of course, when you consider that the money is coming out of the federal treasury, then it must go to as many farmers as possible. Whether the farmer is a big farmer or not, he is still entitled to as much money as the next fellow, when the* money is coming out of the federal treasury. That is something that should be realized by a great many big wheat farmers, who may feel they are due for greater assistance because of the greater volume of wheat they have to sell. They have no more right to more money from the federal treasury than the small farmer who perhaps feeds all his crop, or sells a small amount of grain.
The last time this payment was made, in 1958, the hon. member for Assiniboia called it peanuts, nothing but peanuts. Well, this will mean a great deal in my constituency. It will mean perhaps $1,400,000 spent in the constituency of Acadia this fall. It will mean about 11J cents a bushel for every bushel of wheat sold by western farmers through the Canadian wheat board. Figure it out for yourself. There are approximately 360 million bushels delivered. Divide that into $42 million, and it comes to about 11J cents a bushel. Certainly that is not peanuts to my farmers, and they certainly will appreciate it.
I noticed that the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska was worried about the price of wheat. He read off a great number of countries which were selling wheat, some at lower prices than Canada and some at higher prices. He did not say, when asked, what countries exported and what countries imported. He went on to Rumania, Yugoslavia, and a bunch more countries. Even Switzerland was a net exporter, according to his figures. I never knew of Switzerland gobbling up too much of the export market. On his figures we will agree that perhaps the Canadian farmer is a little lower than the United States farmer. He is higher than the Argentine farmer, and about the same as the Australian farmer. Those are the three big exporting countries. France is now coming into the export picture, and has a considerably higher price.
I know that if the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate were here he would be on his feet speaking about cod and wanting this assistance for his cod fishermen in Newfoundland. To be fair to the eastern members, looking at the dominion bureau of statistics index of farm prices and agricultural products, 1960, No. 6, it lists for June, 1960 the monthly index for the provinces of Canada,

and it is evident that the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are lower than the eastern provinces, and lower than British Columbia.
This is a step that we western members have advocated. We have stated time and again that the farmers need an acreage payment and will appreciate an acreage payment; and because of the subsidization that they gave for Canada to Great Britain during the war and after the war, they felt they had a just claim to it.
It is evident in this same article in the Financial Post of July 30 the way farm subsidies have increased. The hon. member for Essex East said we had done nothing, and the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska said the farmers are just itching for a return to their type of payment. It is obvious that since the year 1957, when there was a change of government, farm subsidies increased from $50 million in 1956-57 to about $116 million the next year, and the following year to $130 million. This year it is estimated that with this $42 million there will be about $122 million directed into farm subsidies in order to bring about better and greater income returns for the farmers.
I am certainly convinced that the farmers wanted this, and they will appreciate it. The minister stated that payments-and I am not going to rehearse what he has already stated- under this type of program will not tend to build up surpluses and will not interfere with marketing. I think that is a point that should be stressed when considering this type of payment over any other type that may be devised.
The hon. member for Essex East said this is a hand-out, but I want to point out quite clearly that it is certainly not a hand-out. It is a payment to the farmers, as suggested in the item which I read out when I started; it is a payment to give higher returns for wheat used for human consumption, and as long as that is coming out of the federal treasury it should go to all farmers as equally as possible.
The hon. member for Essex East said that the government should have called upon the liaison committee of the western farm unions and had a full discussion with them. The government, as the Prime Minister stated yesterday, was only right in contacting the liaison committee after they turned down deficiency payments, wanting some suggestion from them. They were only right in stating, "Please put it in writing so that we can study it before you come down here".
That was one of the objections I had to the farmers' action when they marched down here in February of 1959. If they had sent

their brief down ahead of time the government could have undertaken a thorough study of it. I can well remember the Prime Minister telling the farmers in the Chateau Laurier that if he had had a copy of their brief even the day before they presented it, he could have perhaps presented a better answer to it. That was the very thing he had in mind when he asked the liaison committee to put their views in writing so they could be studied. He said, "We will be able to discuss your problems, if we get it". But they would not. Mr. Wesson got stubborn, or something like that. There was a big press article in the Western Producer, "Why should we devise a policy for you?" They were certainly not asked to devise a policy; they were asked to put their views in writing, which was only a legitimate request, and I wish they had done it. It would have given the government a chance to study it, and I certainly would like to have seen it. But seeing that they never did it I am certainly proud of the fact that we western members continued to press for some sort of assistance to western farmers and were to some extent successful in this.
We could not wait for the liaison committee to send their views. They never contacted me at any time, nor did the farm union president. I had numerous letters from farm union locals. I can honestly say I never received one that came out for deficiency payments. I received a number that suggested we make a payment similar to that made in 1958. They were not too firm in their suggestions. They endorsed our 1958 payment, and suggested that we do everything in our power to attempt to persuade the government to make another one.
That is the sort of thing the farm union locals wanted, but for some reason or other the liaison committee under the direction of Mr. Wesson wanted something larger, something practically impossible to get, so it could be used for propaganda purposes against the present government. There is no denying the fact that they have engaged in a lot of propaganda against this government. Anything they could find to use they were certainly prepared to use. That is the way it appeared to me. I believe they attempted to embarrass the government rather than present a sound argument for additional payments.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska placed figures on the record indicating that farm income was down for the first quarter of this year. The figures indicated, I believe, that it was down so much more in western Canada, $26 million I think it was in Saskatchewan, $4 million in Manitoba and $16 million in Alberta. That only supports the argument that this payment should

be made. I wish to thank the hon. gentleman for putting those figures on the record. They will no doubt be of considerable assistance to him in explaining to the farmers in his eastern constituency why this went out to western Canada. I am certain it will be of benefit to him.
I believe I mentioned that in my own constituency there are over 7,000 permit holders. Mine is a fairly large constituency in the east central part of Alberta. Part of it is in perhaps the driest region of Alberta. My constituency is half dry and half wet, and I am not referring to spirits.
In the northwestern part of my constituency there is a heavy concentration of farming, part of which is made up of small farms where there is a heavy concentration of livestock. In the south there are perhaps larger farms and ranching on a bigger scale. In the east and west there are many straight grain farms. My constituency is subject to drought to a considerable extent, and to hail. While I was home in July of this year a terrific hailstorm swept through part of my constituency. By a freak coincidence the hailstorm followed the same pattern it followed a year ago. By and large the same persons who were hailed out a year ago were hailed out this year, with a few additions. What would they get under deficiency payments? Not very much.
I was talking to a farmer about hail and asked if he were insured. He explained that he collected insurance last year, and because he did so his insurance rate jumped from about 10 per cent to 16 per cent. So he did not insure this year, because he never dreamed he would be hailed out again.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to support the measure announced by the Prime Minister yesterday providing assistance for western grain producers. In doing so there are several points I want to mention without trespassing on the ground that has already been covered, and I would also like to reply to some of the comments made from the opposition benches.
The hon. member for Essex East as usual entertained us yesterday when he replied to the announcement by flailing away in all

Supply-Agricu Iture
directions in the jungle of his thoughts. He then proceeded out into the cow pasture where, blissfully ignorant of where he was placing his feet, he proceeded to plod in all directions. He did indicate, however, that he knew something about cow pastures because he did not forget the bull.
I want to say that this measure providing assistance to western farmers is going to materially assist the transformation that today is taking place. The development of agriculture within the past ten years, the changing over from the old type of agriculture into the "agri-business" has required a tremendous amount of capitalization, and before this government came into office very little assistance in this direction had been received from the previous government.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska in many of the speeches he has made in this house, as well as again today, has referred to the Prime Minister's policies in the two election campaigns. I am glad he did that, because if he were to look at the program that was outlined by the Prime Minister in the 1956 and 1957 campaigns he would discover that the policies outlined at that time have, with the exception of a national rural development and soil conservation program, being largely implemented.
The hon. member for Essex East chided the Prime Minister for bringing in these measures, for talking about crop insurance and farm credit and things of that nature. I think it was necessary that this be done in order to indicate the place this particular program fills in the over-all agricultural policy of this country. I do not think it is possible for anyone to point to any particular measure and say that is the cure-all. We have never attempted to do that, but almost invariably when a measure of this nature is brought into this house the criticism which comes from the opposition benches tends to indicate that they believe, regardless of what measure is brought in, that that measure by itself could cure all the problems of agriculture. Each specific measure that is introduced, and there have been many since this government took power, is designed to take care of a particular situation, and when the entire program has been implemented then we will have that degree of parity that the Prime Minister has spoken of during two election campaigns and indeed on many occasions in the past.
I want to thank the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska for assisting us in our argument supporting this assistance to western grain farmers. One thing which I think we must all recognize is that the western grain producer occupies an unique position in the agricultural economy today, in that the greater percentage of his products find their
[Mr. Jorgenson.1
way into the export market. This makes it extremely difficult to apply measures which we have applied to other products largely consumed in the domestic market. This makes it necessary to develop a policy that is unique in attempting to solve the problems of the western grain farmer.
The hon. member pointed out that during the 1959 crop year the income of the farmers in Canada had dropped by $27 million. He strengthened our argument for an acreage payment when he said this, although he neglected to point out that $20 million of that $27 million was in western Canada. In addition, when he referred to the drop in income in the first quarter of this year and the drop of $50 million, $47 million of that amount was again in western Canada. I might also add here that when he referred to that period he was referring in 1959 to the highest quarter in Canadian agricultural history.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there has been a tendency on the part of a good many people to attempt to relate the price stabilization legislation to a means whereby the problem of the cost-price squeeze-and this is the big problem in western Canada today-can be solved. I submit that this is manifestly wrong. Price stabilization was introduced for a specific purpose, to prevent the uncertainties as to income of the farmers of this country. At the time the bill was introduced the prairie producers of wheat, oats and barley were not included under the jurisdiction of the board, and there was a specific reason for that. Price stabilization by itself is designed to level off violent fluctuations in price and to ensure to the farmer that prices will not drop below certain specified levels. The farmers themselves have an opportunity of discussing price levels with the stabilization board.
To attempt to solve the problem of the cost-price squeeze by the use of the price stabilization board could lead us into serious difficulties. First of all, if it is applied to wheat, oats and barley, as I mentioned earlier a large percentage of these products goes into the export market and we would be using money to subsidize exports. As the Prime Minister pointed out yesterday, that would weaken our argument against those countries which are using that type of sales policy today.
In my opinion the problem of the cost-price squeeze can only be dealt with if you base your calculations on the fact that whatever product is produced must be sold. There are those who conveniently ignore this fact, but assuming that whatever is produced in this country must ultimately be sold, then the problem of the cost-price squeeze can only be met with measures designed to reduce the cost of production-and we have taken

many steps in that direction, and to increase our export markets-or, and I hesitate to suggest this last alternative because it is one that I know will be unacceptable to the farmers themselves, through the imposition of production controls. The United States attempted to use this type of rigid price support in order to assure to farmers their fair share of the national income. Subsequently they had to introduce acreage controls, and rather than getting out of their difficulties they increased them. The government are wise in that they have not followed this course in Canada.
Our product, wheat, finds a ready market in the countries of the world because of its superior quality. It is essential-and I think this is where the government does render a great service-to maintain the quality of our grain and make every possible effort to find more markets for it.
Some time ago the Prime Minister announced that our agricultural policy would follow two parallel but separate lines. There was the over-all policy which was designed to take care of the national situation, and then there were policies which would have to be implemented on a regional basis in order to take care of difficulties that arise within various regions of the country. Obviously a program designed to take care of a regional problem cannot possibly help people in another area; therefore our policy has been designed with that object in view, and we have constantly tried to make the policies complementary.
It is useless to have a program of price supports if crop insurance is not implemented along with it, because no amount of price support can be of any possible value to a farmer who has suffered a crop loss. This is true in this particular instance as well, because during the years when farmers were asking for price support and for some assistance in agriculture they did not have the benefit of crop insurance. I am glad to say that the province of Manitoba has taken the lead in this regard, and in my area a trial program has been put into effect. I might also add here that contrary to the predictions of the opposition, who maintained that farmers would not take out insurance policies, in my own municipality 75 per cent of the farmers have taken out crop insurance. This is an indication of how the farmers themselves support the policies of this government, and it must serve as a reminder to the opposition members that when they were on this side of the house and those policies were asked for they would have been wise to implement them at that time-
Supply-Agriculture
Many arguments have been presented with regard to the specific program now before us, and I do not intend to cover the ground again. There is one particular point in regard to the acreage payment that I wish to raise. I hold in my hand a card issued by the Canadian wheat board which represents the interim payment on the 1957 crop, which amounted at that time to 10 cents a bushel. This card was given to me by a farmer when he came to me and pressed for acreage payments. He said "I have no use for this. It will give you a clear indication, however, of how useless deficiency payments would have been to me". This card is from a farmer who farms a section of land near Arnaud, Manitoba. The total amount of his interim payment on a section of land at that time was $1.33. If he had received a deficiency payment of 30 cents a bushel he would have obtained $3.99. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the $200 which each farmer will receive under this program is by far the better method of distributing this amount of money.
I have received many letters from reeves, councillors, farmers and businessmen in my own constituency, and of all the letters I received from individuals not one advocated a system of deficiency payments. I am not suggesting for a moment that the hon. member for Essex East is supporting a program of deficiency payments on western grain, because he studiously avoided making any mention of it yesterday. We shall be waiting with interest to hear what policy, as an alternative to the one the government has now proposed, he would implement.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the government for providing this measure of assistance to the farmers in western Canada and in particular to the farmers in Provencher who, like many farmers across this country, at the present time are using the facilities of the Farm Credit Corporation, crop insurance, cash advances on farm-stored grain, and many of those other programs the government has implemented since it came into power in an attempt to establish more economical units and reduce the cost of production in an effort to meet the cost-price squeeze and to produce for the benefit of the people of this world. I support this measure, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that the government has arranged for a large number of its supporters to participate in this debate. That, of course, is a right which must not be denied to any party in this house or to any hon. member; but since this is the decision, hon. members will appreciate, of course, that we in the

Supply-Agriculture
Liberal party are also entitled to put forward some views, which will be done during the course of the day, as we are in committee, and as I say since the government has decided to put up such a large number of speakers.
I should like to put on the record now, so that we shall not forget the circumstances which have led to this particular declaration of policy, those events which over the course of a year and a half have agitated the farmers of western Canada in particular, and the members of this house, who have been anxious to ascertain the policy of the government, based on representations which were first made by some 1,000 farmers who descended on Ottawa on May 10, 1959. It is doubtful whether in Canadian political history any policy of a government had its genesis in an event so long removed from the particular situation at the moment as the circumstances which surround this particular policy.
It will be recalled that 1,000 farmers came to Ottawa seeking to elicit from the government some declaration of policy based on promises which the government had made in 1957 and 1958. In 1958 the government announced the same policy we are now discussing. The farmers were going to receive something not consistent with the declaration of "parity, not charity". They were not going to be given deficiency payments as they had been led to believe from speeches made by members of the government and by supporters of the government. Instead, they were to be-

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: In 1958 the government came forward with a proposal precisely like the present one. That was its answer to the farmers of western Canada, an answer that was inadequate from their point of view. Because the farmers recognized that the acreage assistance program of 1958 was not in fulfilment of assurances given during the election campaign they organized this mass meeting, which represented not only one farm organization but the other great national farm organizations. They came here and made their submissions in a manner that impressed everyone, because the Prime Minister observed how orderly and constructive they had been. I hold in my hand a booklet entitled "Souvenir, On to Ottawa", issued by the western farm delegation under date of March 10, 1959, a delegation that came to Ottawa in protest over the failure of the government to implement its election promises and to express dissatisfaction with the inadequacy of the government's program as represented by the acreage assistance program of 1958.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he recall the march to Ottawa in the thirties, when 2,500 western farmers came here to wait on a government of which the hon. member later became a minister? Does he remember the reception that was accorded to that delegation?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
All I can say is
that any delegation of farmers that came to see a Liberal government did not have to wait for a year and a half before that Liberal government announced its policy.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: They had to wait 22 years and still did not get anything.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
This delegation came to Ottawa and presented its program to the government. It was a four-point program, and the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture, in any comment they have made about the representations put forward on March 10, have only referred to one of those requests. It is well that we should put them on the record now, particularly when it would appear that we are going to have an all day debate and so many members from western Canada, as is their right, are going to speak. It is well that we should

have a clear statement of the problem before us. I refer now to page 31 of the booklet, which undoubtedly will some day receive an honoured place in the archives of Canada. The four point program they put forward was as follows:
1.	The first of these is the two-price system for wheat. Under this proposal, wheat sold for human consumption on the domestic market will be priced in relation to the level of the domestic economy ...
2.	We would recommend also that consideration be given to an adjustment payment from the treasury to compensate for the exchange premium of Canadian currency over that of the United States. . .
3.	Farm organizations consider that the cost of carrying grain in commercial storage facilities should be a public responsibility, and not a charge against the farm industry . . .
4.	It has been noted previously that the Canadian farmer is under a severe handicap in the export marketing of wheat as a result of United States subsidized exports policy.
With respect to the last point they conclude with this statement:
Wheat producers recognize the need for the establishment of this policy to hold export flour markets, but they feel it is the responsibility of the Canadian treasury and not of the wheat producer to meet the competition of the United States government.
Hon. gentlemen who have spoken thus far have not referred to any of these requests made by their constituents in western Canada. All they have sought to do today is to indicate that the policy announced by the Prime Minister yesterday is one that attends to the requests and the problems of western agriculture. What they will say to their constituents when they return is, of course, a matter for them to decide, but I suggest that in telling western farmers of this particular policy, now under discussion, they will not be meeting the requests of the farmers of western Canada as submitted to the government in this city on March 10, 1959.
The criticism that we level against the government is not only because of the inadequacy of this present program, but as well because of the way the government of Canada has treated the farmers of western Canada. For over a year and a half it has not been possible to elicit from the government any indication of its reaction to the representations made by the western farmers. The farmers themselves recognized this when shortly after that meeting with the government-I think it was in the month of June-they formed a liaison committee to come to Ottawa to discuss the matter with the government again to see whether a smaller group could prompt the administration into a declaration of policy.
We will remember, that all during the remaining part of the 1959 session, questions were put not by members of the Conservative party but by members of the Liberal
Supply-Agriculture
party and of the group that sits immediately to Mr. Speaker's left. We wanted to know when the government was going to announce its policy or give its reaction to the representations made by the farmers, who came in such large numbers from western Canada. It was not possible to elicit any definite reply, although the Prime Minister did say three or four days before the end of the session of 1959 that the government was giving careful consideration to the matter. He created the impression that some announcement of policy would be made before prorogation. But there was no announcement of policy. So in 1959 there was a denial even of what was done in 1958. No deficiency payments; none of the four points that I have enumerated were recognized; not even this acreage assistance plan was put forward in 1959.
Parliament was reconvened in the month of January, 1960, and it is interesting to look over the record of the attempts that were made by members of the Liberal party to try to ascertain from the government, after eight months, what its policy was in regard to demands made by the western farmers. On the 1st February the hon. member for Moose Mountain, who I believe had to leave the house because of illness in his family, asked a question of the Prime Minister pointing out that a group of representatives of western agriculture met with the cabinet on the previous Saturday, and wanting to know from the government what its reactions were to their proposals. That delegation, headed by Mr. Wesson, asked for the very same things that had been asked in the brief presented on May 10. The Prime Minister's answer to the hon. member for Moose Mountain was that the delegation was advised that a final decision would be announced in parliament within a period of 30 days. The Prime Minister said:
That announcement, of course, will cover not only the whole problem of deficiency payments but as well the several alternatives to which I have made reference.
Then on April 5, 1960 I asked the Prime Minister a question based on an interview given to the Regina Leader-Post on March 5 by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in which the latter suggested that farm leaders should sit down with the government and discuss alternatives to deficiency payments, such as acreage payments. I asked specifically:
Is it the intention of the government to provide acreage payments this year to farmers in western Canada?
That was on April 5. The Prime Minister's reply, in effect, was this. He referred first of

all-and I was grateful to him for this reference-to my wide experience in these matters and observed that I would realize that the only appropriate answer would be that this was a matter of government policy to be announced in due course.
Then on April 8 the hon. member for Assiniboia asked:
Can the Prime Minister say why he has refused to see the western farm leaders, and whether an appointment has been made for some later date?
The Prime Minister replied in effect that the only denial of a meeting was that a meeting could not be arranged before the Easter recess. Yet since that time and in spite of this reply by the head of the government of Canada, no meeting was arranged with the western liaison committee.
Then on May 6, I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he was not going to give some reply to some of the questions put to him, particularly as to the government's intention respecting an alternative program such as acreage assistance. The Minister of Agriculture replied that the western farm organizations were asked-and listen to this-to put in writing any alternative to deficiency payments which they wished to discuss with the Prime Minister and the cabinet. Up to date, he said-

They said, "Here is what we are going to do; parity, not charity. Give us an opportunity and we will devise policies to assist western agriculture." If that does not represent an abdication of the responsibilities of government, I do not know what words constitute abdication. And to think that it was not possible all during this time for the government to meet with the western liaison committee. The government, of course, in not arranging for this meeting with the western liaison committee gave them and this house, and the people of Canada, the impression that it did not want to meet with the western farmers. But the Minister of Agriculture clearly stated, "They must write us a letter. They must make a proposal, and if they make a proposal we will see them".
Yet what have they done now? They have reversed that process. They themselves have come forward with a proposal and now, after the session is almost through, they are going to meet the farmers. Then on May 24 the member for Laurier put a question to the. Minister of Agriculture:
In view of the denials by some leaders of farm organizations, does the minister wish to modify his statement made in the house last week that the federal cabinet had not received any alternative proposals to deficiency payments from farm groups?
The Minister of Agriculture replied that the liaison committee as a whole did not put in any definite alternative as requested in the reply to them by the Prime Minister of Canada.

In view of the advanced stage of the session, is he able to report any progress in working out some scheme to provide assistance to the western grain growers in accord with their request?
Little did he anticipate at that time the many weeks that were yet to pass, weeks of inactivity on the part of this government. Here is what the Prime Minister said:

*-a request has come from the liaison committee of the western farm organizations for a meeting with members of the cabinet. Arrangements will be proceeded with at once for the convening of such a meeting at an appropriate time.
That was on June 9. The Prime Minister said that arrangements would be made at once. No arrangements were made; no conference was held with the western farmers. It was only because of the pressure in the last few days that we have had a reversal of the procedures outlined by the Minister of Agriculture and now, in the dying days of this session, we have this declaration of policy, the same as the policy embarked on in 1958.
Then on June 14 the hon. member for As-siniboia addressed a question to the Prime Minister:
Can the Prime Minister inform the house what progress has been made in arranging a meeting between the government and the liaison committee of western farm organizations to discuss western farm income deficiency?
The Prime Minister said:
I think the question would be more appropriately answered by the Minister of Agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture said:
I have nothing definite I can tell the house at the present moment on that matter.
I do not know that the Prime Minister's suggestion that we could get a definite reply from the Minister of Agriculture proved to be very helpful, but the Prime Minister did succeed that day in having himself relieved of any responsibility for answering a question the reply to which would have been carefully scrutinized by the farmers of western Canada.
On June 24, 10 days later, the hon. member for Assiniboia again put a question to the Prime Minister:
Can the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture inform the house whether the date has now been set for a meeting between the government and the liaison committee of the western farm organizations to discuss deficiency payments, or the government's alternative to that program?
The Minister of Agriculture replied:
The date has not yet been set.
That was the reply of the minister, even though we had been told by the Prime Minister on June 9, that arrangements were going to be proceeded with at once for the convening of such a meeting at an appropriate time. I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question on the same day, June 24:

This is the reply of the Minister of Agriculture:
Mr. Speaker, this has been one of the causes of delay. We asked the western farm organizations

-I think an announcement-can be expected before the end of the session.

speechtext:
My major object in participating in this debate is to assure all comers of this house-although I know one corner is not very well occupied-that this measure which the government is now putting forward arises from the thinking of western members of parliament representing agrarian areas.
The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat used one word very prolifically. That word was "liaison". I began to count the
79951-0-493J
Supply-Agriculture
number of times the hon. member used it but I lost count. He used it several dozen times and I would like to say to him through you, Mr. Chairman, that there is a form of liaison with respect to western agriculture of which he is probably unaware, and that is the liaison that exists between a western Conservative member and the farmers he represents. That, to me, is the highest quality of liaison because it dismisses the political football; you get away from the record and you are not speaking for the record, but sounding the minds of the individual farmers. Those of us who have been here since the beginning of this parliament have had the opportunity-* it is lessened this year-of returning home and talking to our own people, and as we talk to our own people we find that their thinking is reflected in our actions, or perhaps I should put that in reverse, and say that our actions are reflections of their thinking.
This question of a solution to the western wheat problem is not an easy one. This government did not create the problem, and in all fairness let me say the preceding government did not create it. Our problem in the three prairie provinces is one that arises from world conditions. We faced a situation during two world wars when every possible acre in western Canada was seeded to wheat at the behest of the government of the day, and properly so, because after all wheat did play an important part in winning two world wars. Nevertheless, after the last war ended we found ourselves in the very difficult position of having an expanded acreage capable of tremendous production still producing in the face of entirely new conditions throughout the world.
Someone said here the other day that last year the Russians exported into markets formerly shared by Canada some 40 million bushels of wheat. There is our problem. The hon. member for Drummond-Artbabaska today cited certain countries which have developed their wheat production to a greater extent each year. There again is part of our problem. Today we are in a state of flux with respect to wheat and perhaps with respect to agriculture generally. We are still suffering from the economic aftermath of wartime production.
Let me say to you, sir, that the position of a prairie member of parliament with regard to this problem, as with regard to other problems, is not an easy one. Our colleague from Vancouver East, who may have taken the train for the west early this afternoon, said yesterday, that he found himself in the position of speaking not necessarily as the hon. member for Vancouver East but as a member for all Canada. Those of us

Supply-Agriculture
who are discussing wheat here today are in a very similar position; we must think in terms of the Canadian economy and we do so. Though we have all the sympathy in the world for our own people, we come to the realization that perhaps the easy solution, the solution which the hon. member for Essex East has stressed this afternoon, is not possible. We are accused sometimes, as western members of parliament, of lacking sympathy for the western farmer. Nothing could be further from the truth. Our thoughts and our words are continuously directed toward the problems of our own people, and I should like to put on the record-that is a favourite term in this house-the statement that, since the days of the Ginger group headed by my highly respected friend Bob Gardiner, this House of Commons with respect to western problems, has never had a more devoted body of servants than the members of the Conservative party sitting in this chamber today.
Yesterday the Prime Minister in his introductory remarks with respect to this estimate said there was a need to recognize our Canadian regional problems. We do recognize them, and they are many. The coal miner in Nova Scotia has a problem; the hard rock miner in Ontario has a problem; the fisherman in Newfoundland has a problem, and so has the lumberman in British Columbia. Today we are discussing a regional problem in connection with wheat. So far the debate seems to have evolved around the question of deficiency payments versus wheat acreage payments.
Let me say that all of us from western Canada would appreciate the injection into the western economy of $320 million in the form of deficiency payments if this were possible. Unfortunately the Canadian economy does not permit this. Some of us have been here only a very short time, but we have learned some lessons, and one of the lessons I have learned is that there is nothing easier in the House of Commons than to spend the national revenue if you have no responsibility for the spending.
I should like to see deficiency payments paid, but I am firmly convinced it is not in the best interest of all Canadians to pay them on the basis of the representations made by the western committee, however much that committee may be supported by the hon. member for Essex East.
It is idle to say that the march to Ottawa in May of 1959 had no effect. It had a great effect. It had an effect on the thinking of all of us here. I would say as an observer that the birth of the wheat acreage payment

policy, which I uphold, was in part consequent upon the representations made by the western farmers.
We heard yesterday and to some extent today the trade mark "hand-outs". The deficiency payment on the scale advocated would have been a hand-out. This wheat acreage payment in my opinion is not in the same category. We have heard a great deal about the fair share of the national income, and this government has been criticized for its failure to give to the farmers their fair share which, it was claimed, was promised. Let me say to the hon. member for Essex East, with regard to his very pointed barbs concerning the last election, that so far as I am concerned representing a rural riding I made no promises of a fair share of the national income. I made no promises concerning deficiency payments, and I am prepared to go back to my constituents and stand on the record I stood on in 1958, which was that I would represent them, having some knowledge of their problems, to the best of my ability.
I have the feeling that most of us here from the prairies were elected on the same basis. When you pour into the western economy the sum of $80 million, $40 million under the preceding policy and $40 million under this, you are going a long way toward closing the gap between cost and selling price. I would say that this government is to be applauded for the policy it has adopted and for the extent to which this expenditure has been extended.
The hon. member for Essex East-I of course bow to his tremendous fund of knowledge with respect to agriculture; I think it is akin to my knowledge of the automotive industry-took advantage of the opportunity today to criticize the government for the lateness of this approach to this problem. Those of us who reside in western Canada know that some time around April or May you seed the crop and some time around September or October, if you are fortunate, you reap a harvest. The crop at this season of the year is fairly well indicated.
There are tremendous areas in the prairie provinces which have been ravaged by drought. There are others which have been hit by hail. Mr. Chairman, I say that the appropriate time for the announcement of this policy was not last month or the month before, or next month or the month after, but now. Now is the time the western farmer would like to know what measure of support he is going to get from his government, and I am very grateful to the Prime Minister for making it possible for him to know that
now.

I regret the absence today of the hon. member for Assiniboia. In previous debates he has characterized this policy as peanuts. I would be very interested in hearing his comments with respect to this measure, but of course he is advancing his own personal political fortunes elsewhere. Let me relate this policy to my own particular area. I am not now referring to my constituency of Medicine Hat but to my home territory in the eastern irrigation district. We have some 1,400 farmers. They are all farmers with 200 acres or a little better. This policy means pouring into my home locality upwards of a quarter of a million dollars.
Mr. Chairman, that is not peanuts. That is not peanuts for the reason that at the time we did this in 1958 I had merchant after merchant, tradesman after tradesman and municipal authorities tell me how much the entire community had benefited because the farmer had some money to spend. The sum of half a million dollars among 1,400 farmers pays a lot of taxes and a lot of store bills, and I am sure this measure, in my area at least-and 1 am sure this is the general situation-will be greatly appreciated.
We have heard a lot from the Liberal opposition concerning the meagreness of the policy and the delay of the policy. I ask myself sometimes what was the comparable situation when they were in power. I cannot recall any direct assistance to the western farmers by the former government. I can recall a very famous statement made by the prime minister of that government at one time, when he said there was not one five-cent piece for certain sections of the farmers of western Canada, and they did not get that five-cent piece.
We have a situation today where more money has been devoted to agriculture in Canada than ever before in our history. We have a situation today where the position of the western farmers is closely studied day by day by men who live in that area and who know something of it. So I say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, and the members of the treasury benches certainly have my wholehearted support and applause with respect to this policy.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to rise and speak on behalf of the farmers I represent, and to express my gratitude to the Prime Minister for introducing this measure which will provide $42 million in acreage payments. The opposition has tried very hard to minimize and belittle this sum of money, but I can say to you, Mr. Chairman, that to my constituency and to the locality where I live this will mean that
Supply-Agriculture
approximately $40,000 to $50,000 will be paid to the farmers. In my locality $40,000 or $50,000 means very much to many farmers, and more farmers will be able to pay their taxes and put money into the economy of this district.
The hon. member for Essex East has tried to belittle this payment and say that our government has failed to consult with the liaison committee. May I draw his attention to another time in 1946, when the government of that day failed to consult the farm organizations when they made the deal with Britain whereby western Canada-and I stress western Canada-lost $500 million. At that time the wheat pools and the federation of agriculture insisted that they be heard on the matter, but as the records of 1946 indicate the then minister of trade and commerce stated that the pools were not consulted as to the price and the quantity of wheat which was sold to Britain at 50 cents cheaper than the world market price at that time.
I know the farmers did not say very much at that time because they knew they had to help Britain after the war, but the government in charge should have taken upon themselves the responsibility of making these payments on behalf of Canada, not on behalf of the western farmers. It was at that time that the farmers should have marched to Ottawa and demanded the payment of that $500 million.
The hon. member for Essex East said that the acreage payment was a direct relief measure. It is far from a relief measure. As the Prime Minister said when he introduced this measure, it is to be the payment to western grain producers of an amount on wheat used for human consumption in Canada distributed on the basis of $1 per acre to the amount of $42 million. In other words it is the inauguration of the two-price system that we have advocated over the years. Every western member in the house has advocated the two-price system. In my first speech I said that the two-price system is the only remedy that is satisfactory to the western farmers. We know that because of world conditions and trade conditions that exist at the present time we cannot tell our customers overseas what they will pay for our wheat, but we should have the privilege of establishing the selling price of wheat used domestically. Therefore in this regard I would say that this is not a relief measure, it is not a handout, it is a just payment to the western wheat producers.
Just two or three days ago the hon. member for Essex East said that he would support me in every measure I put forward having to do with another grain. I should like to ask him to support me in this measure also.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to this very welcome announcement by the Prime Minister in regard to acreage payments I should like to say it is my belief that a payment of this nature is not only quite justified at this time but will be greatly appreciated. I say this because I am very well aware of the fact that the farmers appreciated the measure in 1958, and I am quite sure they will feel the same way about it this time.
I am well aware of the difficulties facing the people of the agricultural areas of western Canada, and of the fact that the problems which are facing them certainly are not of recent origin. Those problems have prevailed for a number of years, and it is my belief that it is only in the past three years that constructive efforts have been made to arrive at satisfactory solutions.
It is my opinion, as I said before, that the payments which were made in 1958 on an acreage basis were generally very well received in the area which I represent, namely the area of Swan River in Manitoba, which contains around 2,500 farmers. I think myself that the opposition parties must be of the same belief, because we have had a tremendous amount of criticism in the house over the fact that the payments were not made last year. Worthy assistance of this

nature, I believe, is in the category of an extensive regional interest. Therefore it is somewhat improper, probably, for a representative to look on it merely in the light of how it might affect his particular area. I think representatives, therefore, must evaluate this measure in relation to the extent of the aid which will result in the agricultural areas all across western Canada. The sum of $42 million being put into the economy of western Canada, particularly at this time, will be of tremendous assistance. The results of this $42 million, as other members have said, will be apparent not only in the west but will fan out into all parts of Canada.
During the past year I had the opportunity to speak to a number of people from many parts of the west, and I must say that I found them particularly pleased with the acreage payments of 1958. Many problems have confronted the western grain growers over the past number of years, and one of the solutions to the cost-price squeeze which they are faced with is a greater return to the farmer for his produce, as well, of course, as concentrated efforts to increase our export trade. The measure we are discussing today is very closely associated with higher returns to the grain growers for the grain which they produce.
As far as the Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned, it is quite evident to me that the record of the past three years greatly overshadows the export figures of the three previous years as far as the export of wheat is concerned. I am convinced that the Department of Trade and Commerce is not only vitally interested in the job of increasing Canada's wheat sales, but is also doing something about it.
The hon. member for Essex East spent the better part of half an hour presenting one complaint and one complaint only. He complained about the delay in bringing this measure forward. There again I would say that he must be in favour of it when he criticizes the government for delaying its introduction. I did not hear him give his opinions in this regard.

I take it that he, along with other hon. members, is in favour of this measure. Whatever this government has done in the past for western agriculture has been met with howls of criticism from the opposition that it was inadequate and not enough. I should like briefly to mention one or two of the things this government has done since taking office in Ottawa. I should like to mention some of the legislation that has been

passed in support of agriculture. The list includes the Agricultural Stabilization Act, cash advances on grain, the Farm Credit Act, the Crop Insurance Act, amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, increased payments under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the implementation of some of the recommendations made by the commission which inquired into the distribution of railway box cars, sharing in the cost of freight for the movement of fodder and livestock, acreage payments in 1958 and again this year, and contributions to the provinces for unharvested grain in the crop year of 1959-60. Expenditures under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act have also been increased under this administration.
I should like to put a few figures on the record in relation to the measures I have just mentioned. I do not want to clutter up the record with a lot of figures, so I will simply give the total expenditure by the previous government with respect to agriculture in the years 1954 to 1956 inclusive. Money provided by the previous government to support agriculture during that period totalled $272,200,350. Money provided by the present administration during the past three years in support of agriculture totals $556,909,734. If we take a close look at these figures we will see the amount for the last three years is more than double that spent by the previous government in the preceding three years.
To come back to the subject now before the house, acreage payments, it is my firm belief that this measure can in no way be construed as a hand-out. I am certain that the farmers will not look upon it as such, and will make very good use of this most necessary assistance.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS

-who has a
