speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
I would inform the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, if he would take his seat and be patient, that one reason why the farmers of western Canada are so exercised over the conduct of this government is because of the series of speeches made by the hon. gentleman during Easter week when he led them

to believe two things: first, that there would be a meeting with the western liaison committee and the government almost forthwith-[DOT] as soon as he returned to Ottawa he would arrange that-and, second, that there would be some policy, likely one of acreage assistance, rapidly brought into being. That was in April or whenever Easter was this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Would the hon. member answer this question?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Would the minister mind just allowing me to finish this observation which is in the nature of a castigation of the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
Has the hon.
member ever seen an eastern farmer's permit book?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: If my hon. friend had my knowledge of eastern agriculture he would not ask a question like that.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: He certainly would not.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
Surely I have satisfied my hon. friend on that point. May I say this. The hon. member for Provencher mentioned this and he is the only one other than the Prime Minister who did. The hon. member for Provencher referred to the progress that was being made in the matter of crop insurance in the province of Manitoba. The Prime Minister yesterday, realizing the inadequacy of this program, realizing that it was a bagatelle, realizing that the government had been forced into a situation, I am sure much to the horror of the Minister of Finance, in which it had to put forward its best step-and in order to do that it could not have got out to western Canada at this time the suggestion that its policy in answer to the western farmers who came here 1,000 strong was merely this acreage assistance plan-the Prime Minister mentioned a number of things that the government had done and a number of things it was going to do. One of the things it had done was to introduce crop insurance.
I say that the inclusion of that, in the Prime Minister's statement yesterday and its endorsation by the hon. member for Provencher, shows the weakness of the government's policy because as we pointed out to the government last year, the extent of federal contributions in that federal crop insurance plan was of such a level as not to warrant one province agreeing to participate in the scheme, yet the Prime Minister referred to it yesterday as part of a grand program of attack by this government to try to improve conditions confronting the western farmer.
If it was proper to mention that and other things in the Prime Minister's statement and

if there was justification for the hon. member for Provencher referring to crop insurance today, there is an obligation on the part of this government to explain why, after a year, not one province has wholly gone into the scheme. When the crop insurance plan was announced by the Minister of Agriculture it was announced with all the fanfare that attends great and small declarations of policy by this government.
It was indicated at that time that the crop insurance scheme would not encourage provincial participation because of the limited character of the federal contribution and the widespread opportunity given to provincial governments to impose on individual farmers a greater share than they can economically bear in support of the crop insurance scheme. Let the government tell the committee now what progress it has made with British Columbia, with Alberta, with Saskatchewan, with Ontario, with Quebec-

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Ask Mr. Lesage.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
There may be some hope now with a new government there. Let the government tell the committee now what progress it has made with New Brunswick, with Nova Scotia, with Prince Edward Island. The minister has said not a word about this all session. In fact this government has not brought forward any new policy this session, although we have had repeated indications from hon. members who come from western Canada in the throne speech debate, in the budget debate, in written and in oral questions as to the state of agriculture in western Canada and in Canada generally.
The government has brought forward no new policy. It has not even given a report on old policy. We would like to know from the Minister of Agriculture now-and this would be something that would really assist the western farmer and farmers in all parts of Canada-what progress has been made. Is Ontario likely to come into the scheme? Is Saskatchewan? Is Alberta, my hon. friend's own province?
These are answers that will give some substance to the suggestion that this government has a policy with regard to assisting the farmers of Canada. The fact is this. Like on so many other fronts this government, having promised more than any reasonable human being has a right to promise, having been confronted with the reaction to those promises, face to face with the economic problems of the country, just does not know where to turn. For that reason for over a year and a half the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues have been resourceful in finding ways and means of postponing any definite 79951-0-494i
Supply-Agriculture
reply to the farmers of Canada. Not only is that true of western farmers but it is true of promises made to other groups.
The Minister of Agriculture may rise after I have finished and point out that I have made a mistake on some point, and if I have -and I suspect that I may have-I will be the first to admit it.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: I am sure of it.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: But I will say this. I will pit my zeal and my desire to do something to assist the western farmer against what my hon. friend promised and has failed to do. In this policy before the committee now, a policy involving a total expenditure of $40 million-

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Of $42 million.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister said $41 million yesterday. The cost of the program in 1958 was $40 million. Undoubtedly the expenditure of that sum of money is bound to be of value. We all welcome any assistance that will be given to those farmers in western Canada who need assistance.
But let there be no mistake about this: this program is not going to help all the farmers in western Canada. It is going to be of some assistance to some of them, perhaps to a great number of them, but it is also going to be of assistance to farmers with large acreages who do not need this kind of assistance. I ask the Minister of Agriculture, now that we are soon to prorogue, to take a good holiday; to examine his record to date and to place alongside that record the promises of his government; to prepare a balance sheet and, next session, to act forthwith without waiting for prodding by members of the opposition, without waiting to be compelled to give answers, in a way which will reflect a dynamic approach, consistent with an effort of the kind which the Prime Minister in particular and other members on the government side said they were going to make to solve the problems facing agriculture at this its most critical period.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
I think I should attempt at once to save from himself my honourable, learned, but non-agricultural friend from Essex East. The hon. member for Essex East quite evidently, in spite of the fact that we had a program of this kind in 1958 which was debated here for a long time, both at the time it was going through and afterwards, and the fact that we have been discussing this particular matter all day and that it was explained by the Prime Minister yesterday and explained by myself and by several other members of this party today, still has no conception whatever of what the estimate

Supply-A griculture
calls lor and what the program is. He took this break-down and the number of permit holders and looked at it and said that the people who were in the first bracket amounted to 20,323 with 99 acres of cultivated land with on the average 15 acres of wheat, so they would only get $15.
This indicates no understanding of the program at all. The program provides, as indicated in the printed estimates which I think the hon. gentleman has before him, that payments would be made on a basis of $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farmer. The specified acreage of crop, that is the cultivated acreage, is laid down in the wheat board act and is as appears in the farmer's permit book. That is why the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources asked the hon. member for Essex East whether he had ever seen one of these permit books.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Have you ever seen one?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: I have one. As a matter of fact, I deliver grain on it every year.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: I thought you were a hog producer.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
I also have a permit book and I deliver wheat from time to time. There are several of our farmers in the west who do not concentrate all their efforts on wheat or on hogs. We have a somewhat diversified operation.
At all events, the hon. member for Essex East seems to have missed the whole point of the program, that these payments would be made of $1 up to a maximum of 200 acres, so then these 20,323 people will receive an average of $66 each because that is the average acreage they have.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Did you say $66?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Yes. Then the next group would receive an average of $144.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: That's not $200 either.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
No. The payment is $1 an acre up to a maximum of $200. As I said earlier, you take the first three of these groups which constitutes 125,000 people out of 250,000 and they will receive over half of all the money paid out and they constitute the smaller farmers in western Canada. The program which the hon. member has been advocating all along, that of deficiency payments so-called, would have meant that these two groups would have received less than 15 per cent of the total amount of the money paid, and with the third group added around

22 to 26 per cent, the bigger farmers getting the remainder. That is what the hon. gentleman has been advocating.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Now that the minister has been good enough to make this correction, I put it to him right now that on those figures 76,071 holders of permits will receive less than $200.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
Oh well, is that not a complete vindication of the argument
I made?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: No, it has nothing to do with it.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Oh.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: You did not know what argument you were making. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I want to tell the hon. member that he did not know what argument he was making and that he did not understand the scheme. This is a scheme designed to give the maximum amount of assistance we can without giving an outright flat grant of the same amount to everybody in the country of a sum of $200. There is a good reason for this. There are a lot of these smaller farms on which the farming operation is a part-time operation. There has to be some regard paid to the amount of land under cultivation. Some of these small farmers are people who have perhaps only five or six acres under cultivation. But the hon. member apparently thinks there should be just a flat payment made to everybody who holds a permit book or something along those lines.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: That is not so.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Now usually when the hon. member for Essex East is speaking, if anybody interrupts him or asks leave to ask a question he immediately goes into a tirade about an attempt being made to stop him speaking, but now when someone else speaks the hon. member keeps muttering continually.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: I am very sorry, it is only my enthusiasm.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's enthusiasm seems to run away with him continually.
Then the hon. member went on to accuse me of not having said that all farmers would not get the maximum amount. I certainly stated it. I indicated it in the table which I placed on record in Hansard. I said the majority of the smaller farmers would get the maximum amount, but not all of them. There was never any question about that.

The hon. member went on to talk about crop insurance. Crop insurance has nothing whatever to do with this matter but he did ask several questions on the subject, so I would inform him that Saskatchewan last year passed legislation providing for crop insurance and set up a crop commission or an organization along those lines to put a scheme into operation. Then if the hon. member has been reading his local newspapers he would have seen that the Ontario government has been holding public hearings on crop insurance in his own part of the country.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: I know that.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
Just a while ago he was saying that Ontario is having nothing to do with it. Yet right in his own part of the country they are holding these hearings to investigate the need for crop insurance. Alberta has shown an interest in it and British Columbia has also shown an interest. Certainly there is a good deal of interest in crop insurance. When I introduced the bill in the house the hon. member may recall I said that although interest at that time in some parts of Canada might be limited I was sure it would grow, and it is growing, as I indicated at that time.
The hon. member went on to talk about Conservative promises in relation to agriculture. I defy him to produce any piece of campaign literature which we put out in 1957 or 1958 dealing with agriculture and containing a definite promise with regard to agriculture which has not been carried out.
In 1957-58 we brought out our program for agriculture. I have not got it here but it consisted of nine or ten points, and all of those things except one have been carried out. That one was the establishment of a forage bank in the prairie provinces, but the only province which has shown any interest to date is Saskatchewan and any scheme along that line has not been implemented. But every other one of those things we promised to agriculture in our agricultural program of 1957 has been carried out.
While I am on my feet perhaps I had better deal with some of the other criticisms which the hon. member for Essex East made in the first instalment of his remarks today. He said the members of the government had made speeches in the last election campaign to the effect that deficiency payments on western wheat, oats and barley would be paid. I defy him to produce any proof of that whatever. He said that the Minister of Agriculture had said that. The Minister of Agriculture never made any statement of that kind at any election meeting and no other member of the government made any
Supply-Agriculture
such statement to my knowledge. That is pure fabrication, or perhaps I should say imagination, on the part of the hon. member for Essex East.
He also spoke about four alternatives which the western farm delegation proposed in addition to the so-called deficiency payments, but he did not read what the heading was. This is the heading on the brief that the western farm delegation submitted: "Other measures which can be used to limit the need for deficiency payments". They were putting forward these suggestions, which, if they were put into effect, might limit the need, as they saw it, for deficiency payments.
The most important of these, the one which was designed to give the most money to western farmers, was the institution of a two-price system for wheat. The present payments look after that and it is just another means of doing it. The matter of the exchange on Canadian money has ceased to have much effect. The dollar now is down fairly close to par, so the need for that has largely disappeared.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: It is about 3 per cent, is it not?

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Around two, I think.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: Two and three quarters, to be exact.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
It does not make a great deal of difference though.
The matter of the flour would be a very small payment indeed, an amount at the most of $4 million. The biggest of these has been looked after. One of them to a large extent has disappeared, and the third would amount to very little. The fourth one was the payment of all storage charges, and it is a very debatable point as to whether farmers in western Canada should pay no storage at all, because that would place farmers in eastern Canada in somewhat of an invidious position if they had to pay storage on all their products whereas the farmers of western Canada did not pay any storage on wheat, oats and barley. I think that is a consideration of which the hon. member might have thought.
Then the hon. member made a great point out of the fact that we had abdicated our responsibilities because we had asked the western farm liaison committee to put in writing any alternative they wished to discuss with us, and that in our opinion they failed to do so. There is absolutely no abdication of responsibility or anything else along that line. The whole point of asking these people to put in writing the alternative they wanted to discuss, as was indicated to them, was so

Supply-Agriculture
that we might study it and be in a better position to discuss it with them. But there was no question that they would come down here and dictate to the government as to what policy would be put into effect. We said that if they had any new ideas we would be glad to hear them, but they never produced any ideas of value. They merely reiterated the four things they put in their brief to begin with, and then they said that they were also prepared to discuss the acreage payments which we had suggested. As a matter of fact at that time we had not suggested that. But as I say, they produced nothing new whatever, not a single new item for discussion, and as a result there was no particular value in having them come down and discuss all over again something we had discussed with them on several occasions before.
The hon. member for Essex East was trying to make out that we had refused to see them, and so forth. We have seen the heads of these western farm organizations since we have been in power on numerous occasions. We have seen them altogether I think at least six or seven times. As a matter of fact, after they came down with their delegation in March we met them again last January and they presented to us a brief on the 30th of that month, this year. So there has been no lack of meetings with the representatives of western farm organizations, and any complaint along the lines the hon. member has made to the effect that we were trying to turn policy over to them is completely ridiculous. If they had had any new ideas we would have been delighted to have them come down and explain them to us, but they did not produce any.
Mr. Chairman, I believe most of the time taken by the hon. member for Essex East was really devoted to trying to sow the impression that in some way we were not assuming our obligations and responsibilities as a government to look after agriculture, that we were delaying the giving of an answer on this and other matters, and so on. I think the whole record of this government, particularly with regard to agriculture, indicates the exact reverse. We have met the promises which we made before we came into power and have done more for agriculture; we have provided more public funds to assist agriculture, and have started more new programs for agriculture, than the Liberal party did in the whole 22 years they were in office.

maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate on the question of acreage payments. I have been an advocate of this form of assistance for western agriculture and was prior to the march of the farm organizations

to Ottawa in 1959. And I am still a 100 per cent advocate of acreage payments in this regard.
We have listened to the Liberal opposition, particularly today, utter a lot of nonsense. The hon. member did not even know what kind of program we had in 1958. The minister has pointed out that it was obvious, and for the hon. member's further elucidation these people who -have small acreages, from 100 to 199, do not sell their grain.
I would like to give the figures for my constituency in this regard. In 1958-59 there were 1,500 new permits issued in my constituency alone. Why did these people apply for a permit? Why were they not able to sell their grain? Because they were too far from the railroad. In my area we have the lowest elevator storage on the prairies. Those 1,500 people represent almost 25 per cent of the entire farm population of my constituency.
I need not point out to the hon. member that these people would not have got a nickel under a deficiency payment scheme. There is no doubt at all that the argument rests four square on whether we should have a deficiency payment scheme on a bushel basis or whether we should be paying these payments, as we intend to do, on an acreage basis. The Liberal party through its leader has enunciated their policy, as has the C.C.F. party. They have come right out and said they want deficiency payments on a bushel basis.
Let us get the argument right and have them stand on their own feet for a change, instead of listening to the hon. member for Essex East wandering all over the place this afternoon not being able to get back to the point at all. Is the hon. member for it or against it? What program does he want? They had announced that they were for deficiency payments. Obviously they do not know, because they do not know how an acreage scheme works. How could the hon. member bring forward an alternative plan? He could not. Therefore, what we have listened to is just a bunch of Liberal drivel which will sell western Canada down the drain again.
I say that the only reason we have had a substantial increase in assistance to agriculture in the past three years, and particularly western agriculture, is that the right hon. gentleman is leading the government, and the people of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta are going to realize it. They were sold down the drain by the previous Liberal government. I do not say that Mr. Gardiner did not want to do something for western Canada, but he failed to get assistance from the party or from the gentlemen

who are now doing all the talking about trying to do something for western Canada. That is why we did not get the south Saskatchewan river dam at that time. This dam is being built now and it is being built because we have a Prime Minister of this country who comes from Saskatchewan. This is the only way we could have got it.
The hon. gentleman had quite a lot to say with regard to the farm march. It was initiated, instigated, organized and sold by two political parties in Saskatchewan, the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party. Nobody can deny that. Mr. Turnbull, one of the leaders of the march, is now the minister of co-operation in the Saskatchewan government, and Mr. Wesson, a long time Liberal, has been associated with the march to deliberately discredit our Prime Minister in his own province of Saskatchewan. There is no doubt about that. I was one who said that I refused to vote $4,500 to the big farmers on the prairies. The hon. member for As-siniboia went all over the province of Saskatchewan and said that I would not vote this $4,500. My position has not changed one little bit.
The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, a paper which has done more to hold back the development of Saskatchewan than any other that I know of in Saskatchewan-and I was born and brought up there

a paper which has no sense of responsibility, and I can prove that very simply, misquoted remarks that I made in the house. They wrote an editorial without even bothering to read what I had to say. It was something like the hon. member for Essex East getting up and talking about acreage payments when he obviously doesn't understand what they are. This is a paper which has a monopoly in north central Saskatchewan. It is a paper which is supposed to be doing something about the development of Saskatchewan. What has it done for the development of Saskatchewan? Not a thing, sir. I left the province of Saskatchewan because of the socialist government; I am not afraid to admit it.
I now come to the problem which my hon. friends have been talking about. I refer to the liaison committee of the farm organizations. I want to put on record what a farm organization in my area thinks about acreage payments. I have a letter from the director of a large area in my constituency, and I should like to quote from it. I do not intend to give the name of the writer, but I intend to stand by the letter myself:
I was asked to send you our comments on the acreage plan. We are all pleased with the acreage plan which is going to help the small farmers, the ones that need it, instead of a deficiency payment on wheat alone, that would help only a few, and not help the wheat surplus situation any.
Supply-Agriculture
I would like at this time to send you our thanks for your help in getting these two bills passed.
This is from a director of a farm union in my area in Alberta. I have in my file all kinds of letters from farmers in my area, from farm unions in my area, requesting me to vote against a deficiency payment plan and to work for an acreage payment plan as outlined in 1958. I have not one letter from any individual farmer asking for deficiency payments on grain. We hear about what the farm unions are saying. I can tell you, sir, this is what the grass roots of the farm unions are saying. They are saying, we want an acreage plan because it is fair and does not discriminate against initiative and it does not pile up surpluses of the various commodities.
As I said, in my constituency one quarter of the farmers would not have received a nickel under the deficiency payment plan. Why would they not? Because they had the initiative to go out and diversify their operations. I have maintained for a long time that our program to help agriculture must be based on the idea that we have to diversify; that we have to be ready to produce the product that we can sell in the market place. If we do not do that then there is not very much we can do for agriculture.
When the farmers came down to Ottawa Mr. Wesson said that you cannot diversify in Saskatchewan. This year he came down and appeared before the agricultural committee with regard to the question of feed mills. I happened to get him a little bit off the track and I asked this question: Do you not believe that diversification is the basis of the answer to the problems of agriculture in Saskatchewan, and he said, "yes, I do". This was a year later. He is now changing his tune. He now realizes, as he should have realized before, that we must have diversification.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort has pushed the question of rapeseed in this house, and now the hon. member for Essex East is on the bandwagon, and I am very grateful for that. The production of rapeseed is one thing that we can embark on. Owing to present technical facilities and our ability to grow wheat we cannot sell, we cannot afford in western Canada not to undertake two things. We have to recognize and give incentive to quality, but we also have to recognize and give incentive to those people who have the initiative to diversify their farming operations to such an extent that they will be able to have an adequate income from the farm.
The hon. member made a lot of noise about our promises to the farmers. I stand up here and say that this government, headed by the Prime Minister, has fulfilled every pledge

Supply-Agriculture
we made to agriculture. We have not solved all problems yet but we are well on the way to doing it. This kind of program will help.
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver East said we recognize that we cannot do anything about costs. We recognize that something can be done about costs. We have done a number of things to reduce the costs on the farm. First and foremost of these is our new farm credit facilities. Farm credit means better capitalization, which means better management, which means reduced costs. It is as simple as that. Cash advances work in the same way in that they give the farmer the necessary capital to enable him to reduce his costs. Our program of crop insurance, which the hon. member for Essex East has discounted because he does not know anything about what is happening in that field, again is something which reduces the cost of operations and this was brought in by the present government.
I could mention other things such as the conservation conference which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is setting up. Then there are the better and improved facilities having to do with the health of animals, better marketing and research and other technical changes. All of these things help to reduce the farmer's costs and will help more in the future as these programs are fulfilled. To say that we cannot do anything about cost is to say something which is erroneous and not according to the facts.
We have listened, as I have said, with a great deal of amazement to the hon. member for Essex East talking about the acreage plan. It was obvious that he did not understand how it works. I say to him that 95 per cent of the farmers in my area want an acreage plan and have told me so. I told the hon. member so before and he laughed at me. All I have to say to him now is that that is the truth and it will be made evident by support for the government in any future election and support for the Prime Minister as having done more for the three prairie provinces in an historic three-year term than any other prime minister in the history of this country ever did. We shall see that the people of western Canada find out about it in spite of the Sifton press, in spite of the nonsense the hon. member read from the Winnipeg Free Press and that you can read any day in the Regina Leader-Post and in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. Writers from these papers sit in the press gallery and write articles in which they deride members of parliament to stand up on their feet and say what they think. How many times have they ever written articles for these papers in which they have said what they thought?

The figure of 30 cents a bushel was advocated in 1956.
When we announced our statement in the house in August of 1958, which was the earliest we could deal with the matter, we came out with an amount of money which we estimated at that time to be $40 million since the amount of wheat domestically consumed in Canada is between 40 and 45 million bushels, fluctuating each year. We were in effect putting forward almost $1 a bushel even though the wheat pool and the farmers' union had asked for 30 cents a bushel.
This brings up what the hon. member for Essex East was talking about. He spoke about the farm brief and why this government has not dealt with the other alternatives put forward both in the brief presented in the spring of 1959 and the one brought before the government on May 10 this year.

I will repeat what the hon. member for Essex East said because it gives an answer to the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. gentleman raised this question: Do you still believe in the two-price system? The answer is: Yes, I do. But I try to be a responsible minister. As hon. members from western Canada know, those who have the responsibility of putting these policies into practice have some responsibility for the farmers they represent. I am going to point this out. If a payment is made on bushels alone and not on acreage, what happens to the man in the constituency of Jasper-Edson who does not sell any wheat, oats or barley at all? He gets nothing. He feeds his grain. What happens to the farmer in the eastern Manitoba ridings who feeds his wheat, oats and barley? He gets nothing. Therefore, if we are trying to tie our policy towards an isolated problem of the shortage of cash to an over-all co-ordinated and comprehensive program it will be found there has to be some association. If we want to encourage people to move into diversified agriculture, not in a rush but in a steady and economic growth, we are not going to go out and make payments on a bushel basis which will encourage them to go back into the production of wheat, oats and barley.
I know these arguments fairly well. I suggest that what we have done is to take a look at the farmer's rising costs. Even though the farmers asked for 30 cents a bushel in 1956 we gave them nearly $1. What are they asking for now? In the brief dated May 10 they proposed a two-price system for wheat which would add 60 cents a bushel to the producer for wheat used in the manufacture of bread in Canada. The farm organizations asked for 60 cents but we are putting in an item for $42 million which is roughly equivalent to $1 a bushel. We are giving more than what they asked for with respect to this matter in 1960 but instead of putting it on a bushel basis we are trying to find some means that will be fair to all farmers and will be more in harmony with our over-all program as illustrated in the fine speech delivered by the hon. member for Pro-vencher.
I am going to quote from some newspapers, too. The hon. member for Essex East was good enough to quote from some well-known Liberal or Grit papers including the Winnipeg Free Press. I should also like to read from an article in another Liberal paper which is not so "Gritty". I refer to the Lethbridge Herald dated June 18, 1960. I will read a portion from an article discussing the brief presented by the farm organizations to the government:
Three of the four proposals by the western farm organizations are directly designed to raise the

price of wheat. The payment of all storage charges, the creation of a two-price system and the flour subsidy would all serve to increase wheat prices. They would do little for the mixed farmer or for the small grain farmer. They would do nothing for the livestock feeder or for the man who suffered a crop failure. The help would go primarily to the large wheat farmer.
If the federal government agreed to the proposals it would mean they paid the cost of storage on all grain in commercial positions, plus a subsidy on all grain consumed domestically plus a subsidy on flour exports. The annual cost would be about $108 million.
Average production of wheat in Saskatchewan over the past five years has been 20.04 bushels per acre. The subsidy per acre for wheat acreage under the proposal would be $6.60, less a couple of bushels an acre retained for seed, or about $6 an acre.
A farmer who marketed 20 bushels an acre and had 1,000 acres seeded would get a $6,000 slice out of the grain subsidy pile. A farmer with 50 acres in wheat who marketed an average crop would get $300. The farmer who had a crop failure or who for any other reason failed to market wheat would get no part of the proposed $108 million.
Here you have a proposal by the farm organizations which itself, taking those three proposals out of their brief, would be helpful only for the person who produces wheat, because when you pay a subsidy for domestic wheat and concentrate solely on wheat, if you pay a subsidy on wheat flour it goes solely to the wheat producer.
If one calculates what is paid in farm storage and in other forms of indirect payment there would be in the aggregate what would amount to a $6 grain subsidy. This item does not match that, but who would get the big chunk of that amount? The man with the big acreage. You can understand why the Prime Minister told the farm organizations that we were interested in hearing their point of view if they would bring forth a policy that did not discriminate against the small farmer, that would help adjustment to the new type of agriculture we see coming and, in particular, which would not be something which would build up surpluses and help to destroy the very industry we are trying to help.
The farm organizations came back with proposals that seem orientated around the large farmer. Those proposals are now supported by the Liberal party. They are now supported by the C.C.F. opposition. maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext: And you said, see what we have done for the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: SPECIFIED ACREAGE GROUPS AS SHOWN IN WHEAT BOARD DELIVERY PERMITS
speechtext:
We tried to put our story to them. We have not got a powerful press behind us. We have not got a powerful machine like the Liberal party and the C.C.F. have. All we can rely on in Saskatchewan is a few individuals to stand up and say the best thing they can in every street corner of the province. That is what we had to do. We put the facts as we know them before the house and we hope that hon. members from all parts of Canada will recognize the difficulties we have had in western Canada in trying to get the facts before the people.
We say that deficiency payments will destroy the small farmer and we say that if the Liberal party and the C.C.F. keep on with this suicidal policy of supporting deficiency payments that they are out to destroy the small farmers of western Canada and in the long run that policy will destroy the larger farmers, too.
This is not just a debate on an item of $42 million. This is a debate between many of us in western Canada trying to make our voices heard and trying to get across to the people of all Canada that great injustice will occur

Private Bills-Divorce if we follow the policy of paying out hundreds of millions in deficiency payments which will destroy not only the small farmer but which will ultimately destroy the whole agricultural industry of western Canada.

maintopic: JACQUELYN GREGORY BRADLEY WALKER
speechtext:
All the bills are being considered at the same time? I have only one or two thoughts to express with respect to these and my first relates to one of the bills, namely Bill No. SD-341 which was previously order No. 2 and which has now been incorporated. My remarks have to do with the
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
situation which took place last night, a situation which I think was extremely unfortunate because it does make one wonder about what one should do in the future. The hon. member for Halifax when speaking last night, wrapping himself in his flag of integrity and honesty as he did-I think I am correct in raising this under this item because it relates to this one bill-I think unfortunately violated the confidence which all the hon. members of the private bills committee had between them when they made a decision in camera with respect to Bill No. SD-341. A vote was taken in camera, and one of the cardinal reasons for doing things in camera in committee is that no one will violate the confidence of that decision and relate publicly what took place in the committee with respect to any hon. member.
I do not care myself. I am quite at ease to say how I voted on that particular bill, but that is not the point. I do not think the hon. member for Halifax should, as he did and as reported on page 7789 of Hansard, have violated the confidence of the members of that committee which met in camera and indicate how individual members voted with respect to Bill No. SD-341. He also should not have violated the confidence of members of the committee as to how they voted on the Eccles case.
I rose at this point only because the hon. member himself undertook to reveal himself in his cloak of integrity and honesty but then proceeded, as I submit he did, to violate the confidence of the committee in a decision it took in camera. This makes the third occasion the hon. member has done the same thing.

maintopic: JACQUELYN GREGORY BRADLEY WALKER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think I have to answer that. I do not think it is a question of honesty or integrity. It may be a question of very poor judgment on my part, but I do not always hold myself out as possessing sound judgment. But my remarks were not uttered in the spirit the hon. member for Skeena illustrated.

Clause agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often I have an opportunity to speak on Bill No. C-13, respecting the printing of negotiable instruments in the English and the French languages. I come from a section of the country where, as far as my constituency is concerned, about 90 per cent of the people speak English and possibly 10 per cent speak French. We get along very well with the 10 per cent French, and I hope they get along just as well with the 90 per cent English.
We have everything bilingual down there. Even the street car transfers, the tickets, the road signs, the menus; everything is printed in both languages. Therefore I think it would be a great opportunity and a good move to print negotiable instruments in the two languages. I cannot see any harm that that could do. When the majority of the people get a cheque they are not interested in what language it is printed in; all they want to know is the amount. It would not obligate the government to undertake any great expense when sending in cheques to the Queen's printer for printing to add another line. I would recommend that this bill be given consideration and passed. I do not think there is a single hon. member of this house who is not in favour of bilingualism. It is recognized by act of parliament of the province of Quebec and it is provided for in the British North America Act, and I think if the government is going to acknowledge this fact we should go ahead and pass this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill that has come before this house in the same or similar form on a number of occasions, and to me it represents a very laudable objective. The riding of St. Lawrence-St. George which I represent is about 35 per cent composed of those of the French language. In that constituency and in the city of Montreal in which it is situated we have always recognized the principle of bilingualism. As the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Webster) has said, our street signs and practically everything of a public nature that is published in that area are done so in the two languages. Since this parliament was elected we in this House of Commons have given further recognition to the principle of bilingualism by introducing the simultaneous translation system. Some years ago the printed money of this country was changed from being printed solely in English to being printed in both languages. Even in those constituencies where the French language is not used, where possibly there are few if any whose mother tongue is French, I do not think anyone refuses to take paper money because it is printed in both French and English. For many years now I think we have accepted the principle that in this country we have two main compositions of our population, those whose origins are connected with the French language and those whose origins are connected with the English language. I think it has also been accepted that no man should be discriminated against because he is able to speak only one of those two languages.
From my own point of view, I think it very desirable that as many Canadians as possible should be able to speak and understand both languages. Nevertheless, it is not for us to say that because a Canadian citizen is born of French speaking parents and brought up in a part of the country where there may not be too much opportunity to learn and practise the English language he should, particularly in the case of official instruments such as cheques, drafts and so on, which are mentioned in this bill, possibly be put in the position of not fully understanding the kind of document that he is dealing with. It may be

said by those of other views that the cheques which are issued today are pretty well always cashed no matter what language they are written in but I do not think this is a sound argument.
We accepted the principle of this bill when we printed the paper money in both languages. We have accepted the principle of bilingualism in this house and this it seems to me is merely removing one of the last anomalies that exist in our system when it comes to the recognition of bilingualism.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the hon. member who has introduced this bill and to assure him that I wholeheartedly support the purpose intended, i.e. establishing the principle of bilingualism in that field.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like several other members of this house, I represent a constituency composed of both French speaking and English speaking citizens.
The house will no doubt allow me to tell of an historical fact relating to my constituency. At the time of my early youth, most people in the constituency of Brome-Missisquoi were English-speaking, as in several communities in the eastern townships. Today, the situation is reversed, and I now have the honour to represent in this house an electoral district where 75 per cent of the people are French-speaking.
The people of my constituency realize that, under the capable leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Progressive Conservative party is genuinely that of national unity.
As pointed out by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers), already we have established in this house the simultaneous interpretation system; our party has thus confirmed the words of Macdonald and Cartier who said that two languages constituted the real glory and strength of our country.
As several other members have stated, bilingualism is an accomplished fact in our country, and like previous speakers, I take pleasure in congratulating the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) for introducing this bill.
(Text):
It gives me much pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to rise in my place this afternoon and support the bill presented to this house by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Since I represent a riding which is predominantly French speaking it is a great pleasure for me, as I say, to support this bill. Our party, under the direction of

the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) is certainly the party which has done more in the past years to cement the true spirit of national unity than has ever been done before. As we all know-and it has been mentioned many times in this house- the spirit of bilingualism has already been admitted-it does not have to be admitted, it has been emphasized-by the fact that we have put in a simultaneous translation system. If I understand correctly, this system is possibly going to be extended into other areas of our parliamentary life. As has already been said, all hon. members admit and feel most strongly that this bill, which has to do with general cheques and drafts, should command the hearty support of all hon. members.
I should like to repeat in English what I have just said in French. When I was a boy-and I was born in 1928-the district of Brome-Missisquoi was more predominantly English speaking, like many areas of the eastern townships. Today, also like many areas of the eastern townships, such is not the case. I have the honour to represent in this House of Commons a district which is predominantly-I would say approximately 75 per cent-French speaking and therefore, I repeat, it is a great pleasure for me to support this bill. I am proud to say and voice in this chamber that we have a very high percentage of bilingualism in my constituency. I am proud of my constituents. I think of towns like Cowansville, Bedford, Farnham, Sutton, Knowlton and many others where both languages are spoken perfectly. When you hear them speaking English you might think their mother tongue was English and when you hear them speaking French you might think their mother tongue was French. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the spirit of bilingualism is more than an intellectual proposition in my constituency. It is something that is deeply believed in and deeply felt. I feel I have a very strong mandate to support the bill now before the house.
It was the spirit of Macdonald and Cartier in 1867 that brought about the union of two great races and two great languages to form the glory and the force of our country. Time and time again the Prime Minister has made that clear from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Today we see these unifying forces. Today that message means two great languages and two great cultures as well as many other groups. I think particularly of people in western and central Canada who have come there from far distant lands to form part of the glory and force of Canada today. The spirit of Cartier and Macdonald, today, as symbolized by the Prime Minister, includes people whose ethnic origins are in many distant lands.

Although coming from the far province of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, I was very fortunate in the early years of my life to live in the city of Montreal and to receive some of my basic education in that city. So I feel that to a certain extent I have an understanding and a knowledge of the French speaking people from the province of Quebec.
I have a great admiration for the French language. As the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) has said, it is the language of culture; it is a language that has a softness and tenderness, as compared with the English language. I feel that we in Canada are extremely fortunate to have, under the British North America Act, the bilingual nature that we do have.
I think I shall draw to the attention of the house before I proceed any further the fact that our fathers of confederation in 1867, in the British North America Act, made an explicit provision for the fact that there were going to be two languages in Canada. Section 133 reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from the court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
I feel that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) in introducing this particular bill has done us a great service, because he is in fact giving effect to the recognition which is already in the British North America Act. I feel, too,

that it is also important to consider whether this act is within the legislative scope of the federal government. In the provisions of the British North America Act I think we have every assurance that it is under our competence and jurisdiction, and I would refer Your Honour specifically to section 91 of that act. That section reads as follows:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms in this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
I would point out, that the particular subsection in which we are interested is subsection 18, which deals with bills of exchange and promissory notes.
We have therefore established through section 133 and section 91, subsection 18, of the British North America Act first of all the jurisdictional right of the parliament of Canada to enact this particular legislation. I suggest that section 133 provides the cultural justification for the enactment of this particular section. I feel the fact that we have two languages in Canada is not a division, it is not a bifurcation; but I think it provides for greater unity and understanding between two great races and two great nations.
I think this was recognized by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he introduced the system of simultaneous translation, because I have noticed since my arrival here that with the advent of simultaneous translation English speaking members are now becoming quite fluent and proficient at French, and the French speaking members, who seem to have a greater aptitude for catching on to English very quickly, seem to be also benefiting materially by this particular system.
I feel too, that being in the city of Ottawa and so close to the province of Quebec there is the opportunity to obtain many of their cultural benefits. One of the most enjoyable forms was the one where the Quebec members very kindly extended their hospitality to many of the English speaking members to join in the celebration of le bonhomme carnaval festival in the province of Quebec last year. We were able to see first-hand real French Canadian hospitality. We were also able to try out our French on a very understanding and sympathetic group, and we were also able to understand many of the joys of what I would like to call la belle province.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to make a few comments on the bill now before us. As some hon. members will recall the principle of this bill or a similar bill was approved on January 31, 1958, I believe, when a vote was taken on the bill then before the house and the four parties then represented in this chamber voted in favour of the principle of the bill. There were a number of hon. members who voted against the bill independent of party. The house having voted for the principle of the bill indicates that there is a general approval of the principle of the extension of bilingualism in this respect. Those hon. members who were here at that time will probably remember the colourful speech of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small).
Perhaps in the past not all areas of Canada have readily accepted the idea of bilingualism. However, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) has reminded us, section 133 of the British North America Act accords the right to Canadians to use French or English, the language of their choice, in the particular fields delineated in that section.
As history developed various extensions of this principle have been made. As we have been reminded today the paper currency of this country has been made bilingual. I believe that the prejudice which has hindered the development of bilingualism is rapidly dying out in Canada in large part because of improvements in the means of communication through which contact is achieved between the people of the two major races. In my own riding there are not many French speaking Canadians and as would be true of similar ridings in Toronto many languages are spoken. Next to English the second largest language group would be Italian, I believe.
Historically, Canada is bilingual. I think it is a good thing that we recognize this principle and sincerely practise it. One of the great handicaps of the English speaking people of Canada has been the fact that they have not learned other languages as readily as have Canadians of other racial origins. As a result we have lost a great deal.
During world war II, I had the privilege of serving with a New Brunswick regiment that had both English and Acadian members. I got to know those of Acadian ancestry very well. In our brigade we had members from Quebec. In those years of trial and

challenge we grew in respect for one another and for the customs, desires and hopes of each other. We came to realize that regardless of racial origin we shared the desire to build one Canada, a nation that would respect the freedom for which we were fighting and the customs of the people within the country regardless of the province in which they lived.
We came to realize too that as our country opened up through immigration from various countries across the world we must develop a new tolerance. We grew in understanding of the idea that ours is a young country that would meld together various cultures to develop the Canada for which we were fighting.
In spite of the prejudice that may exist in certain sections that perhaps have not had the benefit of close friendship and association of other language groups the trend toward bilingualism continues to grow. In permitting this growth the country broadens its horizons and enriches its social fabric. When one learns another language it is like obtaining a key to new knowledge and new understanding.
For the reasons I have briefly stated I wish to add my support of the principle advanced by the proponent of this bill. Although in my riding we do not share in the proportion of French speaking Canadians that may be found in some other areas in Canada I believe we do share the same aspiration and hope that this country will continue to respect the rights of those of different religions and cultures.
Those who are in favour of the extension of bilingualism must attempt to respect and understand the feelings of those who at the moment perhaps hesitate to fully endorse the idea of the extension of bilingualism. Through your understanding I am sure you will succeed in sharing your ideas with them and in winning their support. Be not discouraged by delays or misunderstandings that may arise from time to time because fundamentally, I think, we are united from coast to coast as one people with one purpose, to abide in this country, the land of freedom, in mutual respect for the individual rights and privileges of all.

Mr. Chairman, just before five o'clock I made a rather reluctant beginning and pointed out that the farmers of western Canada had been waiting for some indication from the government that some of their problems would be relieved, not necessarily on a short term basis but on a long term basis.
When I was in western Canada I visited a number of farmers before and after the march to Ottawa and I was very surprised to find that members here representing those ridings said that the farmers were pleased to accept the acreage payments when they were paid in 1958. I found that was not true of the farmers I talked to. Whether other hon. members talked to a different group than I I am not in a position to say, but in the main those who received acreage payments in 1958 accepted them because there was not anything better and they needed the money. They did not agree that this was the solution to their problem. They knew the problem would be the same next year and that probably it would get worse.
I suggested to them something which did not come to pass. I suggested that they would make the march on Ottawa, that they would get their 300,000 signatures and receive a hearing, but I suggested that they would go back home and would have to report that nothing came of that march. I also predicted at that

time that the next year again they would receive an acreage payment because it appeared to be a very good political gimmick, and that the acreage payment they would receive in 1959 would be $1.25. I expected that in 1960 it would be $1.50, and that by the time the Conservative government went to the people again this acreage payment would have reached proportions probably of $2 an acre. I realize, even if the government does not, that if they are going to give a hand-out on a relief basis they will have to increase the relief as the need increases or it will not even be of any value as an election gimmick.
The western farmer, being no different from any other farmer, is not particularly interested only in the problem as it affects him today but also is interested in correcting the problem on a long term basis. Farmers all across Canada have a large investment in land, in equipment, in buildings and the farm itself and they know that as time goes by there is only one solution for their agricultural problems and that solution is not deficiency payments or acreage payments but a parity price which can be applied to all agricultural products. Farmers have realized, and I believe also the Prime Minister has realized, that there must be eventually a long term solution which will put agriculture into a much more favourable position where they will not have this declining income and rising costs which they have had over the past few years.
When this delegation came to Ottawa a pamphlet was published on March 10, 1959 by the western farmers delegation, and it pointed out the following:
Other groups in Canada have faced comparable increases in costs. But most of them have been able to pass these increases along to others through higher wages or through increases in the price of goods and services they sell. The grain farmer, however, has the price of his product fixed in the export market. Consequently, he is unable to adjust his prices to domestic cost increases over which he has no control.
The rising spiral of costs has been the most significant factor contributing to declining farm living standards. Farm organizations have long held that the government of Canada must accept responsibility for the policies which have permitted a spiralling of farm costs. Consequently, if they are unable or unwilling to arrest this spiral, the government should be prepared to accept responsibility for maintaining farm prices in some reasonable relationship to costs .. .
The government has recognized the danger. Its proposals looking toward a long-range corrective program are appreciated. These policies may eventually place agriculture in a position to cover its costs. But, until that time arrives, the grain producer must be assisted.
Then they point out three ways in which they consider the farmer can be assisted, and these are as follows:
1.	Expansion of export markets. This would be helpful to the extent that farmers were able to increase their marketings. The majority of farmers

in the west will have no grain on their farms by mid-summer. Therefore, they would not be helped immediately even if expansion were possible.
2.	Reduction of farm costs through lower prices of goods and services used on the farm. This would call not only for price controls, but for pushing these prices back to the level of ten years ago.
3.	Transfer payments from the treasury to increase grain prices through deficiency payments.
When these 300,000 people asked the government for assistance they realized that even if they got deficiency payments this would not solve their problems on a long term basis. They were suggesting that other methods more applicable to them would solve the problem instead of acreage payments.
It has been pointed out that the grain farmers do receive other assistance. The hon. member for Essex East pointed out today that this amounts to $150 million, and I do not know whether that is too high or too low. But there are other factors which enter into the problem and there are other considerations which should be given to the grain farmers of western Canada.
We have never really attempted to solve the problem which affects agriculture, not only in the grain industry but all other industries as well, and until this government comes up with a constructive agricultural policy applied to all agriculture it will not get the support of the farmers of this country and it is not going to deserve the support of the farmers of this country.
Acreage payments will do two things. The payment of $1 an acre does nothing to overcome the cost-price squeeze; that is, the worsening of the farmers' position by continuing to increase the cost of production. It is this cost-price squeeze which today threatens the agriculture industry.
Second, the $1 an acre payment smacks of a hand-out or relief measure because it is based on nothing but political expediency. It means no more than the payment of five cents a bushel which was made in the hungry thirties. If you take the average as 20 bushels per acre, you will find this amounts to exactly the $1 which was paid by the then government in the depths of the depression.
Third, $200 in relation to a farmer's total expenses and cost of living is a trivial sum. The Prime Minister claims that it helps the small farmer, yet a small farmer with less than 200 acres receives less than $200. It was pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon that there will be 76,000 people in western Canada having an acreage affording them less than $200 under this acreage payment. There will be 125,000 who will get $200 more or less.
Deficiency payments have been an alternative which has been put forward by the
Supply-Agriculture
farmers of western Canada themselves. They admit that deficiency payments will not solve the problem. They point out that the government must immediately initiate a trade program which will encourage the selling of more grain produced by the western farmers. Many farmers who are producing and selling grain on the quota basis depend on the sale of that grain for their income, and their quota this year is seven bushels per acre. I would suggest, that the costs, calculate them as you wish, on the average farm in Canada cannot be covered by the sale of seven bushels of wheat per acre, and the costs of production cannot be geared to a seven or eight bushel quota.
On the other hand, deficiency payments do help to develop a parity price in grain production. To me a parity price means an amount sufficient to cover the cost of production and to pay to the farmer sufficient to enable him to have a decent standard of living for himself and his family. Deficiency payments have these advantages.
There is a clear-cut case for deficiency payments, based on the Prime Minister's election promises of parity of income for farmers. By refusing or failing to control the farmer's cost of production the federal government has a direct responsibility for his present difficulty. Therefore, by making deficiency payments the government would discharge its responsibility to the farmer.
Deficiency payments mean in effect an increase in the price of wheat, oats and barley sufficient to provide a compensation for the increase in the cost of production and therefore strikes at the root cause of the farmer's difficulty, namely the cost-price squeeze. Deficiency payments would constitute the kind of major policy necessary to assure the survival of the wheat industry so important to the economy of the three western provinces. Payment of deficiency payments of the magnitude requested can be practically applied, since the alternatives that the delegation has put forward, for example payment by the federal government of all storage charges, payment of a subsidy on flour exports and, the two-price system, would automatically reduce the cost of deficiency payments.

They are going to demand-and they have every right to do so-that an over-all agricultural policy be developed which will solve some of their problems rather than just cover them up. Among those problems is the major one of the cost-price squeeze. This government is going to have to do something either to increase the price of wheat being sold internally and externally and at the same time reduce the cost of production of the farmers, or-

Mr. Chairman, the simple
answer is no. I am not completely unfamiliar with the problem, though. As the minister knows, we have set up a committee to study the cost of farm machinery and his own members from Saskatchewan and others have pointed out that there has been a study of the co-operative ownership of farm machinery. There has been a study in the province of Saskatchewan of whether we should reduce the amount of farm machinery being used, whether it is possible to get along with less machinery. I am familiar with the fact that certain studies have been made. The minister will probably be happy to know that in Ontario also this problem has been given consideration. One of the conclusions that we have come to in Ontario is that a considerable amount of the land that was opened up for agriculture a number of years ago should be turned back to forest production. Perhaps the minister is also aware of the fact that in Ontario, as I presume in the west, we have given consideration to the size of farms. This in turn increases the costs that the farmer has to bear because it has become apparent that he needs more land.
I hold in my hand the supplement to handbook of agricultural statistics put out by the dominion bureau of statistics, dated March, 1960. It points out that the trend in the prairie region is in the direction of larger farms. In 1901 the average size of farms in the prairie region was 279 acres; in 1911 it was 289 acres; in 1921 it was 344 acres; in 1931 it was 381; in 1941 it was 438; in 1951 it was 498; and by 1956 the average acreage was 546.
So, this matter is not completely unfamiliar to us in Ontario. This is one of the reasons why we say that $200 is not a fair amount to be paid, that the acreage is not large enough and that a large number of farmers who are in a marginal position are not being given a large enough acreage payment to be of any value to them because they have had to increase their acreage very rapidly over the last few years. In rising to ask a question the minister has only pointed up what I have been saying, that this problem is a growing one. The government of Saskatchewan is giving consideration to it and I am quite sure the governments of other provinces are also doing the same thing. We are pleased that they are.
We suggest that the federal government should not only hand out this $200 by way of relief, which everybody needs and will be happy to receive, but should also come to

the conclusion to initiate a study so that we can arrive at a long term agricultural program, which the Prime Minister himself indicated they were going to do and on which he considers they are now working.
In this regard, I suggest that what has been done so far as crop insurance is concerned has been unsatisfactory because only one province has shown any great interest in that program. In our over-all approach to solving the problems of agriculture we have depended too often on such things as five cents a bushel per acre or the $1 per acre that we are now going to pay. The farmers will welcome this payment. We are willing to support it but I inform the government now that my discussions with farmers of western Canada and my understanding of the situation indicate to me that this is not a solution for tomorrow but only for today. The farmers are unhappy that the government did not see fit to make this type of payment last year and if it is going to be an election gimmick next year the payment will have to be more than $1 an acre.
