maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. The only reason I referred to it was that it helps to make a more economic unit in so far as the farmer's business is concerned.
[The Chairman.]
Some reference has been made to crop insurance today and the fact that it is not more universal in this country at this time. We waited for this more years than most of us would like to remember. Last year when that legislation was put on the statute books it will be recalled there was a situation in western Canada that brought more vividly to the minds of the people in that part of the country than anything else the need for that kind of legislation. I see you are getting a little restive, Mr. Chairman. I am not going to pursue that particular subject at this time but I did want to mention that.
In addition to these things, reference was made today to the South Saskatchewan river dam, a project designed to take care of a situation in that arid part of the province of Saskatchewan where a greater diversity of production is required than exists at the present time.
It is also notable, that in 1960 the provinces received over $500 million more than they received in the last year of Liberal rule. For my part, I cannot possibly go along with the hon. member for Essex East when he says that farmers who were farming on a larger scale do not need any assistance at this time. All of them, large and small, need all the help that government legislation can give them, to provide them with the opportunity to secure an equitable return for their products and labour.
If we go back to 1958 when the acreage payment was made we will see that there are those in western Canada who said they did not know that that payment was related to the two-price system for wheat. I have here a report dated September 4, 1958, in the Western Producer, the official organ of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and it says this:
By rejecting the principle of basing the domestic price of wheat on Canadian costs and Canadian living standard, the farmers are requested to subsidize the users of bread. This means that 18 cents of the 21 cents loaf is based on Canadian costs and living standards, the three cents share which goes to the farmer is based on a subsidized wheat price with the farmer doing the subsidizing.
How could an organization make a statement such as that in the face of the statement that was made by the Prime Minister at the time the legislation was brought forward in parliament? The hon. member who preceded me did not think this government had been very successful in reducing the wheat surplus. I have a report here which appeared in the Star-Phoenix last year under the heading:
Wheat Surplus Now Felt at Manageable Proportions By Board Chairman McNamara
Mr. McNamara said Canada had reduced its wheat surplus by 200 million bushels in the 1957-58 crop

year. He thought there would be a corresponding reduction during the present 1958-59 crop year ending July 31.
There is another aspect of this situation about which I should like to remind the hon. member for Essex East. He referred to the pamphlet, "Souvenir, on to Ottawa". I have a copy here and on page 2 I find the following:
The grave situation in agriculture began to develop after 1954. At the end of the second world war, when price controls were removed the cost of goods and services required by agriculture began to climb along with all other costs in Canada. Up to 1954, the price of wheat and other grains shared to some extent the generally buoyant price levels. That is, the rise in costs was partly offset by better prices for western grains.
After 1954, however, the price of grains began to go down. Meanwhile costs continued high for a year or two and then, in 1955 and 1956, began to rise rapidly as the Canadian economy headed into a new wave of expansion. The result spelled trouble for the grain producer. As his costs went up, prices for his output went down and he was caught in a squeeze which increasingly threatened his economic existence. It was in this situation that small groups of farmers throughout the country began to demand policies which would rescue the grain industry from the threat confronting it.
What was the answer of the Liberal party? Even during an election campaign their only answer was to try to bribe the farmers of western Canada, with their own money, by offering them a 10-cent increase in the initial payment. Before I conclude, I should like to say that I think it is generally recognized that farmers throughout the world are suffering today from the cost-price squeeze. This was very ably brought out on January 14 by the vice president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Mr. Bobier, when he spoke to the field husbandry association at the Bessbor-ough hotel in Saskatoon. He said then:
Farmers not only in Canada but all over the world are feeling the cost-price squeeze.
Alf Gleave, the president of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, had this to say:
Limited sales and limited production are putting farmers in a strait-jacket. . . and increasing the size of farms will "not rid us of our headaches". The solution lies in faster movement of grain out of terminal elevators, and the key to this is "stepped up efforts to boost export sales".
Anyone reading these words, and I have almost 100 clippings of one kind or another dealing with this situation, cannot help realize that not only the farmers but the farm organizations have recognized the fact that there is a great deal of confusion among themselves with regard to what the solution to the problem may be.
I wish to say once more that there will be those who will say that this payment should have been larger. For my part I am happy to see the government resume the course it set out upon in 1958. I would encourage those
Supply-Agriculture
on the treasury benches to follow through in the years to come and implant this estimate more permanently in the statutes of our country.
One thing is certain. The Liberal party has learned nothing from its defeats in 1957 and 1958. I have referred already to the fact that their answer to the problem was a 10-cent bribe with the farmers' own money. After listening to them in this debate I am convinced that they are opposed to acreage payments and that they are opposed as well to aid for western farmers because they have not offered any alternative to what the government has proposed at this time. I am proud tonight that I am a Conservative because to my mind this payment represents the supremacy of parliament so far as every western Canadian member of parliament is concerned and because I know that the principle of this payment put forward by the government represents the considered opinion in western Canada today. No one will go to western Canada and say, as the C.C.F. and the Liberals are saying and have been saying, that there is no principle in this estimate. I also believe that this whole experience, and I emphasize that it has been an experience, will inspire western members to continue their representations on behalf of their electors. I shall support the measure and I will be surprised if the opposition dares to oppose it in a vote or even by way of an amendment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with considerable interest to the hon. member who has just taken his seat. It is obvious that in the period since the hon. member made his courageous onslaught against the government and its farm policy, by process of attrition, he has come to regard the government as being now closer to his position than he thought it was on that famous occasion. I rise now simply to refer to a statement made yesterday in Saskatchewan by a representative leader of the farmers of western Canada who I know will be looked upon as expressing a very important segment of western farm opinion. Indeed, the hon. member who has just spoken referred to Mr. Gleave and referred to him approvingly. In tonight's mail I have received a copy of a statement made by Mr. Gleave yesterday which has a very direct bearing on the subject under discussion. The statement is dated August 8, 1960, and reads as follows:
"The $1 per acre payment for western farmers announced today in the House of Commons by Prime Miniser Diefenbaker is small compared with the needs of those farmers", A. P. Gleave, president of the Saskatchewan farmer's union, said here today.

Supply-Agriculture
"It is regrettable that the Prime Minister did not find it worth while to meet with the western liaison committee as we had requested repeatedly", Mr. Gleave, who is chairman of the committee, said. "Only 10 days ago, we received a letter from the Prime Minister's executive assistant saying that such a meeting would be arranged."
The liaison committee had informed the Prime Minister by telegram in April that it was prepared to meet with the government to discuss acreage payments as an alternative to deficiency payments which had been rejected, Mr. Gleave said. This was followed up by a brief on May 12, receipt of which was not even acknowledged by the government. The brief outlined an annual income deficiency of $109,700,000 for western farmers, and repeated the request for a meeting.
"We are happy to see some result of our efforts, but by taking such unilateral action the government obviously intends to assume full responsibility", Mr. Gleave said. "It will be up to each and every farmer in the prairies to judge for himself as to the adequacy of the government's action."
This is a statement from the president of an important national farm organization. Mr. Gleave comes from the same province as does the hon. member who has just spoken. The hon. member said he was satisfied that west-tern farm opinion would support the position he has taken tonight. I call in answer to that statement the statement of Mr. Gleave who is now in western Canada and who is presumed, I believe, to know a good deal about what the farmers of that province and that section of Canada think.
Let me tell my hon. friend for his benefit that we have already stated in the house that inadequate as this measure is we recognize that the farmers of western Canada need assistance and to the extent that this assistance will help them it is being supported by us. But like Mr. Gleave, we say it will be up to each and every farmer in the prairies to judge for himself as to the adequacy of the government's action.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I wonder if the hon. member for Essex East realizes that Mr. Gleave, the head of the farm union in Saskatchewan, has actually fewer members in his organization than I had supporting me in one constituency, one out of 17, in the last election. That is how many people he represents in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Since I am asked a question by a very amiable and disin-guished gentleman of this house I have no hesitation in answering it. I do not know anything about my hon. friend's organization. I hope it is a good organization. He will require a good organization, because when the next election comes, not only he but many hon. members from western Canada are going to require good organizations to meet the opinion that exists among western farmers in regard to the government's agricultural policy.

I do not know whether my hon. friend's organization is stronger than Mr. Gleave's. But I do know Mr. Gleave and I believe him to be a knowledgeable and responsible farm leader. I have in support of that statement no less a person than the hon. member for Rosthern, who spoke only a few moments ago in such complimentary terms of this farm leader Mr. Gleave.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Chairman. I wonder if the hon. member for Essex East realizes that the Conservative members, 17 of them down here, are the political representatives of the farmers of western Canada, and not Mr. Gleave.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I make no apology at all for rising for the first time today, not the third, to express on behalf of the 11,000 farmers in the Wetaskiwin constituency their appreciation of the announcement of the Prime Minister of the payment of a dollar an acre. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Essex East who spoke so favourably of deficiency payments, and also to my friends of the C.C.F., that deficiency payments would have been paid to less than 1,000 of those farmers in my constituency. The acreage payment will be paid to every one of them.
The hon. member for Essex East gave me the information in the course of his remarks quite some time ago that there are 224,717 permit holders in western Canada. Perhaps the hon. member does not know that the scheme of deficiency payments which he so strongly supports would have put 87 per cent of the money in the hands of 14 per cent of the farmers, whereas this method of assistance puts this acreage payment in the hands of every one of those 224,717 farmers, large or small.
The people in my constituency, will appreciate this. I will quote a newspaper article now for the edification of the hon. member for Essex East, who today took great delight in quoting a statement of a constituent of mine, a friend and a neighbour, the president of the farmers union of Alberta some time ago this year. He said as quoted in today's Ottawa Journal:
It has not solved all the difficulties-
And this, we make no claim to doing, but we do make a claim on behalf of this government of trying to help western agriculture. Mr. Nelson goes on:

but it is something to work on.
I should just like to quote this also to the hon. member who is so fond of quoting newspapers and newspaper authorities. Mr. Ransom, president of the Manitoba federation of agriculture, said:
Very acceptable ... but temporary relief.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: A very good man.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Another quotation is:
Even though small, it will be well received.
That was the minister of agriculture for the province of Alberta. As the hon. member knows, they are not supporters of this government. I think perhaps the most eminent authority in western Canada on farmers and farm problems is the president of the United Grain Growers Association of Canada, Mr. J. E. Brownlee. He said:
The distribution of some $40 million among farmers in western Canada will afford considerable relief, particularly to small farmers.
Of the 11,000 farmers in my constituency over 80 per cent have an acreage of 300 acres or less. So I say again that 1 am expressing on behalf of the people of my constituency, and I am sure of the province of Alberta, their appreciation to this government for having recognized their needs and having taken these steps to ease it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to make a few brief comments on this particular item in the supplementary estimates. As I represent an agricultural riding from Manitoba I was very pleased with the announcement made by the Prime Minister yesterday when he announced this one dollar per acre payment to farmers in western Canada.
Some members have referred to this payment as being a hand-out. It has been referred to as a hand-out by speakers from both the Liberal and C.C.F. parties. But in reality it certainly is not a hand-out. One can call it a subsidy. The very wording of the supplementary estimates indicates that. The wording is as follows:
Payment of an amount, as a higher return for wheat used for human consumption in Canada, to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely:
$1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres par farm in accordance with regulations-
Et cetera. So therefore you can say it is a subsidy. In my constituency most of the farms are quite small. In a large section of the constituency there is very, very good land and production is high. In other parts of my constituency there is marginal land and the production is low. In this case with an acreage payment the farmers will get the same return per acre, while under a deficiency payment the man who had a large yield per acre would benefit much more than the man on the marginal land whose crop was smaller.
This afternoon the hon. member for Churchill outlined the legislation that has been introduced by this government, and it was a long list. I do not intend to repeat it here,
Supply-Agriculture
but I just want to point out that all that legislation that has been introduced by this government is aimed at bringing stability into the agricultural industry, and given time to work it certainly will bring about that stability. Some people get a little excited because they do not see any immediate effect. But all that legislation which the hon. member for Churchill referred to this afternoon will in the long run bring about stability in the agriculture industry. This one dollar per acre which we are discussing tonight certainly is another step in bringing stability to the industry.
The hon. member for Essex East referred several times today to the fact that this has not been adequate, that it is inadequate. There are those who will always say, regardless of what the amount is, that it is not sufficient. We know that is only human nature, that no matter what you get you always want a little bit more.
Also in his speech this afternoon the hon. member for Essex East said the Prime Minister said yesterday this program would cost $40 million. On page 7743 of Hansard, the Prime Minister in his speech mentioned that the program would cost between $41 million and $42 million, and this is based on the assistance program of 1958. This type of subsidy would certainly help the small farmer and the so-called family farmer. This government at all times has shown great interest in the family farmer, those people who actually live on the land and farm themselves. That is the type of farm which we have to try to maintain. We know that the small farmer today is facing many difficulties not brought about by himself, this government or the preceding government, but brought about by the great technological changes which have taken place in agriculture during the past 15 years. This government is facing up to the situation. It is attempting to find a solution to the great problems created in the last 15 years.
This measure of acreage payments along with other legislation this government has introduced during the last three years is certainly providing assistance to the farmer and is helping to ease the problem. We have not said that the present measure is a cure-all. I have not heard any hon. member of the government make that claim and I am sure no government member would make it. Certainly, however, this measure does represent a step that will be helpful to agriculture. This sum of $42 million when spread out across western Canada will benefit not only the persons who receive the money but the
7862.

Supply-Agriculture
business people in each area. It is a real shot in the arm for the economy of western Canada.
It has been said that in the west we have 48 members of parliament, 47 of whom are Conservative members. If you take away the hon. members representing urban ridings such as Winnipeg which has four seats, Calgary which has two, Edmonton which has three, and Regina and Saskatoon-11 in all-that leaves 37 rural constituencies. If you divide 37 into $42 million that averages over $1 million for each rural constituency in western Canada. That certainly is not peanuts, it was referred to by the leader of the C.C.F. group in 1958 as such. The payment of over $1 million for each rural riding in western Canada will be of great benefit to the farmers and to all the people of that part of Canada.
I am sure the farmers in my riding will appreciate the $1 an acre payment. I also know that there are many who would have liked to have seen a larger payment and who perhaps feel that the present payment is not sufficient. Nevertheless I am sure that each and every one of those farmers will be very glad to receive this payment and the amount that each receives will be of definite benefit to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it affords me great pleasure to be able to rise and speak on vote No. 576 and to express my appreciation and the appreciation of the farmers of the constituency I represent to the Prime Minister and the government for this assistance the farmers will receive. It will be very well received in my constituency and while the payment of $1 per acre up to a maximum of $200 may not be as much as some had hoped for, it is, I am sure, as much as most of the farmers expected. When I heard the Prime Minister-if I heard him aright

tie this payment in with a payment on the wheat used for human consumption in Canada I realized that it would be tantamount to the payment of about 70 cents a bushel for the wheat that is consumed in Canada. That will be of great assistance to the farmers and will be equivalent, in effect, to the establishment of a payment for a two-price system.
This payment cannot be called a deficiency payment such as was asked for by the mass farm delegation that came to Ottawa. The farmers in my riding realize that the deficiency payment asked for by that delegation would have been of little use to the vast majority of my farmers. A few would have got all the money that would have been received in my constituency.

I was a little surprised to hear the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and the hon. member for Essex East make so much fuss about this payment. It would seem that they were jealous of the fact that they were not doing it and of the fact that the government of which they had been members had never seen fit to assist the farmers of western Canada to this extent. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska mentioned that he was looking forward to the return to power of a Liberal government. I should like to suggest to the hon. member that while he is waiting for that supposedly wonderful day to come about he should not hold his breath until it arrives.
I was somewhat amazed at the would-be righteous indignation and the air of injured innocence of the hon. member for Essex East-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Why go after him all the time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
-especially when he started in to remark about the lack of agricultural policy on the part of this government. I recall attending a meeting on March 26, 1957 which was addressed by the former minister of agriculture. He was, I am told, the only member of the former Liberal government who knew anything about what was going on in his department and he was Mr. Agriculture to the Liberals. At that meeting he stated the Liberal government's policy. It was this, that the farmers in Canada never had it so good up to that time. He also said that anybody who could not raise hogs at a profit for 19 cents should not be farming. He said he could do it. I hope he is finding out what the score is now.
Another point that interested me is that both opposition parties are trying to make so much out of the fact that in three years in office this government has not been able to quite clear up all the mess that was made while the Liberals were in office for a period of 22 years. Is it not about time they realized that it takes a little longer to clear up the mess they made such a good job of creating? They say that this payment is too little, that the small farmers are getting less than $200. What would those small farmers have got had the so-called deficiency payments for which the farm organizations asked been introduced? They would not have got a nickel out of it, because they would not market enough grain off a quarter section to make any money in that way.
It is not very often that I try to indulge in any political backbiting in this house, but tonight I have found it expedient to do so and that is just in order to help keep the record straight. I shall not take up much more

of the time of this committee, but I do want to commend to all those who read Hansard the contributions which have been made on this item by hon. members supporting the government. There have been quite a few made already and there will be more made during the course of this evening. In all those addresses there has been very good material, very true statements which should be spread around throughout the farm communities of this country.
Again I want to thank the Prime Minister and his government for bringing this matter forward, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I accord it my most sincere support. I thank you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with those who have spoken before me in appreciation of the announcement made by the Prime Minister that acreage payments will be paid to western wheat growers this year. I do not want to repeat what has been said by speakers who have preceded me, but I am certain this will be welcome news to farmers and to the businessmen who do business with the farmers. There should be around $1 million paid into my constituency by the acreage payment method. We do not believe that this is a cure-all but at the same time I do not think it is peanuts, either.
This acreage payment should help to alleviate the effects of the cost-price squeeze in which the farmer finds himself owing to the high cost of farm machinery, of fuels and of machinery repairs. I think this method of payment is fair because it does not discriminate against the farmer who feeds his grain and it does not rule out the farmer who loses his crop through weather hazards; the man who, in my estimation, is the one who needs a payment the most. Lastly, it does not encourage an increase in wheat production, and I think this is important in the light of the surplus we have at the present time.
In view of the correspondence which I have received during the last few months, I may point out that the requests for acreage payments exceed by far the requests for deficiency payments. In conclusion, I wish to say that I endorse and appreciate this payment to the western farmers. Thank you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I rise at this time to say a few words on item 576. I shall try to make my remarks as brief as possible, because I realize there are others who are to follow, and I believe the ground of this subject has been fairly well ploughed. However, I have a few remarks which pertain to the feelings of the farmers of my constituency, and may I say that during the past three months I have
Supply-Agriculture
received a total of 11 resolutions from F.U.A. locals in my riding and, in addition, a large number of letters from individual farmers. Now each of those locals were prompted by the F.U.A. central organization in the province of Alberta. In so far as the F.U.A. locals are concerned, they were asked by their central organization to write to their member of parliament and to suggest an alternative to deficiency payments. I have received these 11 resolutions and I have since had an opportunity to talk with many of the members in these different farm organizations in my riding. I have been working among them to ascertain their desires, and may I say that in all cases they have asked for acreage payments.
The vast majority of farmers and particularly the small farmers do not want deficiency payments. I say this in answer to the hon. member for Essex East and to others, especially those in the far corner who have spoken in favour of deficiency payments. The majority of farmers in my riding are not asking for deficiency payments. They would, of course, like to see a somewhat bigger payment, that is true, but did hon. members ever hear of anyone who was perfectly satisfied with any particular payment? I imagine that if we were to make a canvass of them they would all be grateful, and many of them are very thankful for the payment of $200, especially when they realize that the payment is one which is being made to them and which is not being all paid out to the large producers.
While I am on my feet I want to say that the western liaison committee to which the hon. member for Essex East has often referred is a committee which was formed supposedly to speak for the farmers of western Canada. But the committee does not hold the confidence of the grass roots farmers. They are not speaking for the farmers. There are too many motives back of what they are doing which are not held by the people they are supposed to represent.
There is an evolution going on in agriculture. Yes, there is a very definite evolution in agriculture, and if you are to understand the farm problem of western Canada you must break it down into its elements. There is the large, medium and small grain farmers, and I have 6,000 farmers in my riding. About one third of all the wheat produced in the province of Alberta is produced in the Macleod constituency, so I have some right to speak on this subject.
If you break down these 6,000 farmers into size groups as I have done they follow a pattern which is about the same as was outlined this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture. About 60 per cent of them are

Supply-Agriculture
small farmers, and it is this group that we seek to reach by this acreage payment. As everyone knows, there is a storage payment which amounted last year to $38.9 million and which went to wheat producers through the wheat board. That, in turn, is a payment for the storage of wheat, oats and barley and amounts to from 6 to 10 cents per bushel. This storage money goes indirectly to the people who deliver grain to the wheat board. To be sure, some of it goes to the small farmer but the great bulk goes to the large operators. It is not only fair that this $41.3 million under item 576 of the supplementary estimates should supplement the income of the small farmer; it should go all across the board, and include the small farmers.
It it were possible to single out just the small farmers I believe the large farmers of western Canada would go along with the proposition, if it were administratively possible to help the small farmer to a greater extent because it is the small farmer who is finding it most difficult in his struggle against the cost-price squeeze. There is perfect competition among farmers. As everyone knows, the farmer operates in an economy which is, I must say, perfect in its competition, and he does not know he is in competition with his neighour.
Under this sort of situation the advantages of technological improvements are not retained by the farmer but are almost immediately passed on to other larger groups. I mention that as a justification for making this payment to farmers, and it has its roots in the economic phenomena of the perfect competition environment. So I say to anyone who wishes to help the position of western farmers that prime consideration should be given to that.
With regard to this payment of $41.3 million, perhaps 230,000 permit holders will receive approximately $200 per farmer; but in the aggregate it is a tremendous amount of money, and in my riding alone will amount to about $1,200,000. If you take communities where there are 500 farmers, at $200 per farm this would amount to $100,000 of additional purchasing power in the community. This sum should give a stimulus all along the line to small businesses and to all others in that area. For those reasons it is not only supported by the farmers but it is supported by all those who must rely upon the farmer and his income for a livelihood in those agricultural areas.
Let us analyse for one moment one or two of the statements made here today about what this government has done and link them up with the income of the farmer. I want to refer briefly to on article in the Financial Post of July 30, 1960, page 3. That

article shows the incentive subsidies and the income subsidies over the years. In 1954-55 they amounted to $41.6 million; in 1955-56 to $51.4 million; in 1956-57 to $44 million; in
1958-	59 to $116.9 million; in 1959-60 to $130.1 million; and in 1960-61 will amount to about $120 million or $130 million. In other words, there is 300 per cent more subsidies going into agriculture today than in the years between 1954 and 1957 under Liberal administration. How can the opposition and the hon. member for Essex East in particular answer that question and say that this government has done nothing for agriculture?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I never said it did nothing. I said it did not do very much.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Let me pass on now to one or two other matters and then I shall close and yield the floor to others. I should like to see the time when the farmers of western Canada receive $2 a bushel for their wheat. If it were possible to bring about a situation where wheat surpluses were taken care of and the farmers received $2 a bushel for their wheat, with a balanced economy and a greater population it would provide the farmers with the type of income they need. I do believe that inside of another 15 or 20 years there will be sufficient growth in population to take care of the productivity of the farms of western Canada and give these farmers that type of price for their goods.
However, as we all know we are faced with competition in world markets. We have had international wheat agreements. Every effort has been made to maintain prices to the farmer, and I just want to quote the price of western wheat No. 1 for 1958-59. The initial payment was $1.40; the interim payment was ten cents and the final payment was .09374, the farmers receiving in all a little more than $1.59 per bushel. The
1959-	60 crop is expected to yield to the farmer for No. 1 wheat in that neighbourhood too.
So that the operation of the wheat board, which is a government monopoly is doing a grand job for the larger grain farmer. What he needs is larger quotas and a little more money would be helpful to bring him up to the international wheat agreement level; but he is not as badly off as the small farmer who we are trying to reach and help with this acreage payment. So I say that there is every justification for this acreage payment and I advance this argument believing that this payment is well conceived by the government and will be deeply appreciated by the farmers.
I might add that the province of Alberta, which has tremendous wealth by way of natural resources, which has a provincial budget of more than $325 million and about

80,000 farmers, might also give some consideration to matching the federal contribution of $200 per farm which would cost them about $16 million and bring the income of the farmer up to, say, $400, which would be something I am sure all the farmers would appreciate.
One other point on the cost of production side. The hon. member for Timiskaming said that the government should control the cost of production. I should like the hon. member for Timiskaming to tell me how he or anybody else could control the cost of production on my farm or on any other farm. It is beyond control of any government. If you are going to assist with the cost of production of the farmer it is necessary to go into the question of the price of farm machinery. An investigation is under way on this subject and hearings will be held next session and we are hoping that the results will be useful and helpful to farmers in the cost of machinery side of their operations.
This government has added new legislation like crop insurance, paying 20 per cent of the loss, and also this government instituted farm credit; and I need not go over all the other items which this government has put into effect.
In closing, may I say that there are 230,000 permit holders in western Canada. There are so many of them that if the government was to attempt to raise the level of each one to the point where I, and I am sure many other hon. members would like to see it, it would be a tremendous burden and it might place the industry itself in a position of instability. On the other hand, if the world surplus could be eliminated and we could by some means balance the supply and demand for wheat and get the farmer a price through that particular avenue I am sure that he and everyone else who depends upon agriculture would be tremendously benefited.
The government has made a tremendous move forward. The new programs which have been put into effect are costing over $100 million. In addition we come along with another $40 million in assistance to the agriculture of western Canada and when we get our story properly across to the farmers they will understand. They know about it because they have met in each of their particular locals and talked things over. They are extremely intelligent; they know the story just as well as all hon. members know it. When the story is told to them in an unbiased way they will certainly be 100 per cent in favour of the policies put into effect by this Progressive Conservative government during the past two or three years.
Supp ly-A gricu Iture
I met a delegation of farmers last Friday evening and I never heard a more enthusiastic group. They know that this government has given them every piece of legislation they have asked for in the last 50 years with the exception of deficiency payments. I can verify that by saying that I was once the president of the junior branch of the united farmers of Alberta, and built an organization of over 6,000 young people. Let me tell the hon. member for Essex East that we do not need to ask him about the problems of western agriculture. Farm people are starting to understand and speak up in favour of the things which this government has done, and show their appreciate because they know that the majority of the fine pieces of farm legislation which are on the statute books today and which agriculture is enjoying were put there by this Progressive Conservative government.
I should like to make a few remarks about cattle prices and then I am through. There was a floor price of $17.80 on good steers put in effect on April 1, 1959. Hon. members may ask what effect it has had since the price has been higher. It has helped those farmers with their income and I am relating it to the income of ranchers as well as farmers. This floor price is simply to project the income of those people who are trying to make a living by producing whatever types of commodities are best suited to their area.
One rancher came to me about two years ago and he was about ready to contract and to sell his calves on a five-year basis for 20 cents or 21 cents per pound, and he asked me what I thought. I said to him, "you know there is a new and improved farm floor price in effect; you can add the price of cattle together for the past ten years, divide it by 10 and multiply the result by 80 per cent and you have the floor price." Instead of this rancher going into the program and contracting his calves for the next five years he said, "No, I will take a chance; I will stand on my own feet with the help of the price stabilization act." What has happened? Two years ago he sold his calves for 32 cents a pound. Last year he sold them for about 27 cents a pound. He has made oodles of money as a result of not going into that contract and if it had not been for the price stabilization act he would have signed the contract.
Therefore, I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to those who are inclined to criticize, that those acts may need some truing up, they may need some adjustment to fit the needs of agriculture, but they are doing a grand job. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and all those who

Supp ly-A griculture
assisted in bringing this legislation into being. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on his announcement of the acreage payment and to assure him and others that it has my full support.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I add a
few words in support of this measure. In my constituency, which is one of the two in Canada that enjoys irrigation on a grand scale, the other being the constituency of Medicine Hat, represented by my colleague, over half a million acres are under the ditch. The farms are small and specialized compared with the large grain farms, and thus a larger number of farmers benefit from this type of government action than would benefit by a straight deficiency type of payment. These farmers would benefit only to a small extent from another type of payment owing to the fact that they grow and subsequently sell only a small amount of grain; in fact, just enough in many cases for their own use.
The point I want to make is of course that this announcement is more than welcome in my area owing to the fact that there are more small farmers and what we commonly call family farms than anything else. There is also the fact that a diversified area benefits from the announcement. No matter what the farmer specializes in, the acreage payment is by far the most equitable and the most desirable way for the government to fight the high cost of production that our family farms are experiencing today.
Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize that I feel quite strongly about the preservation of our family farms. These are not just farm units or a statistic, but a way of life in Canada that we in this house should be very much concerned about at all times. Very soon we shall have to concern ourselves to a much greater extent than we have in the past before the present government took office.
The present government, as we all know, has done a great deal along this line for agriculture and I must pause for a moment at this time to give praise to our Minister of Agriculture. Naturally, I am very proud to call him our minister and doubly so because I sit on the same side of the house as he does.
Without going into detail I just wish to say that it was largely through the efforts of the minister and his colleagues that western Canada in particular sent Conservative representatives to the House of Commons in Ottawa, not only as supporters of the government, but as members of the government. I can tell hon. members in this house that not only as a western member but as a farmer myself I have all the confidence in the world that the

problems of agriculture, and particularly of western agriculture, will be dealt with properly and that this government will do a great deal along this line.
As a matter of fact, having listened often to hon. members opposite I should remind them of just a few of the products that are being stabilized under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. However, I will not take the time of the committee to go into detail because the statistics are available and well known to most of us. I am sure that even the hon. member for Essex East would have most of the statistics available if hon. members opposite would only consult him.
I wish to point out the greatly increased participation by the government in dealing with the cost-price squeeze that faces agriculture. As a matter of fact, when total expenditures are compared in the years immediately prior to and after the present government taking office we find that in some cases they were almost tripled by the present government. This bears out that the government has been very seriously and successfully doing a great deal toward solving the dilemma that confronts Canadian agriculture.
In considering further just what the particular payment now under consideration means, may I point out that the sum of money involved has been referred to by some hon. members opposite as a mere pittance, peanuts, and other such phrases. But I ask you, Mr. Chairman, can hon. members opposite describe that amount of money, which represents taxes collected from the people of Canada, by such phrases? I cannot do so and, as I said before, as a western member, as an actual farmer, I can only term this move toward equalization by the government and the amount involved as a very serious financial effort to come to grips with the problem that exists.
I also feel that by the time the next session begins further serious considerations will have been given to the alleviation of the pressing financial problems with which Canadian agriculture is faced. The provision of an acreage payment at this time is a most welcome and timely move by the federal government. I need not tell the committee what cash in the hand of western farmers means. We all know quite well how many times a dollar changes hands and assists the whole economy of a community. I have heard it said that by the time the circle is complete a dollar has changed hands something like eight times.
The hon. member for Essex East stated that the government has ignored the requests of the farmers of western Canada. May I remind

him once again that there are several members in the house representing western farmers who are in close touch with their constituents and are actual farmers themselves. I am a farmer, a member of parliament, and if the hon. member sincerely wants to know something about western agriculture I suggest that he should ask some of us who have spent a lifetime engaged in western agriculture.
In a truly diversified area such as mine with small farms specializing in such crops as peas, beans, alfalfa, sunflowers, onions and sugar beets, the grain farmers specializing in grain alone fulfil a need in rounding out the full circle and are not a deteriment as some people try to say. All the people in the whole diversified cycle benefit from a payment of this type.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a farmer and one who represents a large farming community I feel it is my duty to take part in the debate on this very worth-while item. Many farmers in my constituency, as well as people in all walks of life, will be very happy at the announcement made by the Prime Minister yesterday. Acreage payments will be very well received and, I might add, are greatly needed at this time by a large number of farmers. I am most pleased that the Prime Minister and the cabinet have taken heed of the views of western members of parliament, the many farm organizations and individual farmers who have requested acreage payments.
Many farmers and businessmen have been in favour of the two-price system. However, they realize the difficulty in making payment under such a system on a bushel basis and the danger of increasing wheat production. Because of that fact they feel that the measure now proposed is the fairest way in which payment can be made. I would take issue with the members of the opposition who spoke when the announcement was made yesterday and referred to these acreage payments as relief. This is not relief but is something that is due to the western farmer because of the price squeeze situation in which he finds himself and what he has to pay for the commodities he requires to operate his farm.
The government has brought in many measures which will assist agriculture. The government made an acreage payment on the same basis in 1958 which I know was appreciated by a great many farmers and businessmen. I am quite sure that a similar payment would have been made in 1959 if it had not been for some organizations that wanted to embarrass the government and put forward the idea of deficiency payments
Supply-Agriculture
which would have cost some $325 million. They knew that the government could not accept this proposal inasmuch as it would have assisted the large grain producers to the greatest extent in that about 87 per cent of this vast sum would have gone into the pockets of about 27 per cent of the farmers.
I am aware that the proposal now before us will not be a cure-all for the problems of the western farmer but it will be a great help. I sincerely hope that the inquiry being made by the agriculture committee into the high cost of farm machinery will bear some fruit and that the item now before us will help the farmer to solve many of his problems. In conclusion, I should like to say that I fully support and endorse the acreage payment program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, down through the years there have been many discussions in the house of the problems of prairie grain farmers, particularly wheat farmers. I have sat throughout the entire debate and I must say I have never heard a better treatment and consideration of this continuing problem than that which has taken place today. I think it has been an excellent thing that so many western members have had an opportunity to contribute to the discussion because unfortunately there has been an attempt to convey the impression throughout the country that members from the western constituencies were not doing the job of representation that they had been sent to Ottawa to do.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: They have been prodded by the Liberal members.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Notwithstanding that attempt to malign these hon. members I think it has been demonstrated that we have a very high standard of representation in the house. I am not going to speak at length tonight because during the years when I sat in the opposition I made many speeches on this important subject. The last major speech I remember was only three years ago, which is not a very long period in terms of history. At that time I urged the then Liberal government to launch a new program for Canadian agriculture. Those were the days when the minister of agriculture of that time was endeavouring to convince the farmers of Canada, particularly of western Canada, that they had never had it so good. Furthermore, the then minister of trade and commerce, a minister who bears such an important responsibility in matters pertaining to wheat farmers, was even denying the necessity at that time for a cash advance program.
I think it has become apparent here today that our western members are intimately and

Supply-Agriculture
closely in touch with the problems of our prairie farmers. The only criticism that we have heard, repeated several times in the discussions from across the way, have been to the effect that this program is to meagre, it will not solve all the problems of agriculture. Second, that there has been too much procrastination in launching the program. Those criticisms have been answered over and *over many times. As a matter of fact, when we consider the long delay in coming to grips with agricultural problems of the former administration, obviously they need no answering whatsoever.
Much has been made today of the fact that this acreage payments scheme does not represent the true viewpoint of the prairie farmer. X have taken the trouble over the past three years to keep very closely in touch with the viewpoint of farmers in my constituency. I have met annually with the representatives of the farmers union. I have received many letters and have corresponded at length with representative farmers, particularly the president of the Manitoba federation of agriculture who was quoted here tonight by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.
Typical of the expression coming from those sources, especially in letters expressing the viewpoint of individual farmers, is the notice of a meeting that took place in the town of Antler last April. This was a meeting held by the Saskatchewan farm union last April 7 at which Mr. Gleave spoke. At that meeting a motion was passed favouring acreage payments rather than deficiency payments on grain, in this way assisting all farmers. Antler is a typical agricultural community, and the viewpoint expressed in this formal resolution coming from that meeting is the viewpoint that I have heard expressed time after time in reference to the issue that we have been discussing here today.
The Conservative government has launched a new program, a national program for agriculture, that we in opposition during the years I sat in this house advocated year after year. This is not a new problem. As a matter of fact, I came into this house as a result of the growing protest back in 1951 because of Liberal inaction on growing agricultural problems.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Surely not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I was competing against- and the hon. member for Essex East knows this-the dean of agriculture of the University of Manitoba, and the crux of the campaign at that time was the growing problems of the farmer. Nothing was done until 1957. We have made tremendous progress since that time, and I believe the item we have been

discussing today is another long step forward in assisting the farmer, who after all will have to bear the real burden of solving his problems, in moving to a new period of prosperity in the agricultural industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not a farmer; I am not a farm expert, but I am a representative from western Canada in this parliament of Canada. I am one of 47 the premier of Saskatchewan referred to some months ago as members who had never been heard of before, who had not been heard of since. He is a pretty good friend of mine. I realize that was a political sally with a bit of a barb in it, and I will not take him to task too much for having said that.
I do say this, though, that I have not cluttered up the pages of Hansard very much with words. I came here to act responsibly on behalf of my constituents and Canada as a whole. I will be quite satisfied to do that. The courses of action open to me have been courses which I could follow behind the scenes, courses which did not bring newspaper headlines, but courses with which I have been satisfied. They have brought the results I have been seeking, and as long as I can take that sort of action I will not speak very often in the house.
However, I feel obliged to rise on this occasion after listening to the debate today, particularly to the great expert of the Liberal party who put forward indignant criticism of the measure, made with such sincerity as he always evinces whenever he speaks on any subject, on any side of any subject, or in the middle even of the course that is being followed. I could not resist the opportunity that has been given to me to say a few words at this time. In his criticism the hon. member for Essex East directed some remarks to the delay of the Prime Minister and the government in taking no action in regard-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: "Procrastination" is the word I used.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
to a meeting with the farmers liaison committee of western Canada. I have suggested to him before when I have spoken, and I suggest to him today, that people in glass houses should well consider before they throw stones.
I think when he talks about delay in government action he should turn his mind back to the many, many years when the party of which he is such a capable member sat in this house as the government, and the delays that occurred then. I heard in 1919, I think, a Liberal spokesman put forward the idea of a national health scheme. Any action in that regard came, it seems to me, just before an election was called in 1956.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I know it is getting late and the patience of the hon. members of the opposition is growing a little thin. I have listened diligently to the debate all day and am content to let the matter rest at this stage.
Coming from a business community in western Canada I feel I can say that this measure is welcome indeed for it will be of assistance not only to the farming community of western Canada but will make an impact on the business community of western Canada and eventually on the business community of eastern Canada. The impact will be very great indeed. I venture to say without being guilty of exaggeration that the final impact on the business community will be in an amount seven or eight times the amount we are voting here tonight, an amount of $294 million in its effect.
In closing let me say that I have confidence in the government of which I am a backbencher. That term does not bother me a bit. I have an opportunity to play my full part in that category and to represent my constituents well. I came here because I was interested and because I was confident that with the leader of the Conservative party we have there would be every expectation of curing many of the ills created over the years under the previous Liberal administration. We have made a long forward stride in that regard. The criticism coming from opposition benches and the concern they have for the future of this government is of little value and is of not very great concern to me.
They talk about unfulfilled promises and the promises that brought us here. I think on reflection they should consider that it was not our promises that brought us here. We were brought here by the lack of action on the part of the Liberal government over a period of over 22 years. The actions this government has taken I am convinced will have the effect of maintaining the confidence of the people whose support we will win again on the next occasion we go to the people for a mandate. I support this measure wholeheartedly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: We have no objection to the Minister of Finance seeking to reply. It will not be the first time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The item is not carried.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may we have an answer from the minister?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East asked what the amount of the supplementary was last year. I have not got that information here as I explained to the hon. gentleman. I said I would be very glad to obtain it and send it to him and I think that should be sufficient under the circumstances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The minister may think it is sufficient but in this committee each hon. member must take his own position and accept his responsibility as he sees it. Can the minister tell us whether or not the supplementary estimate last year was as high as this year or was it less?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I have no recollection of whether it was larger or smaller than this.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: What was the total expenditure on this item for the last fiscal year both in the main and supplementary estimates? What amount was being spent?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Last year, as far as the main estimate was concerned, it was $433,510; that was 1959-60.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: What was the supplementary?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: As I say, I do not know what the supplemenetary was. I cannot carry these figures in my head as the hon. member well realizes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister is asking the committee to vote a supplementary item and when asked a simple question as to what the amount was last year he complains that he cannot carry the figures in his head. There can be no criticism of him for that but there can be criticism of him for not doing the committee the courtesy of bringing the information with him when he comes before us with this estimate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have already said I would get the information and supply it in response to the hon. member for Essex East. All that hon. members opposite are doing this evening are engaging in obstruction.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Oh?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the minister has stated that we are now engaged in a process of obstruction. This coming from a minister whose estimates have been attended tonight by a whole series of speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite for the sole purpose of preventing this house from voting on amendments having to do with old age pensions-*

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: On a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I can only hear one point of order at a time, but I must remind the hon. member for Essex East that he must not impute motives to any hon. members.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Withdraw.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You will recall that when points of order were raised earlier tonight there was not the same vigilance despite the obvious fact that hon. gentlemen were violating the rules of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Order. I cannot permit the hon. member to proceed along that line in criticism of the Chair. He may do it tomorrow if he wishes after he has consulted the record. I do not think his comments are fair and I shall not tolerate his continuing along that line.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
On the point of order-
Supply-Agriculture

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: My point has not been dealt with. The hon. gentleman charged us with obstruction, and I have asked you to ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: There is no point of order involved in that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
rose on a point of order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am speaking on the point of order at the moment. I do not think there is any point of order involved, but if the hon. member takes such objection I will gladly withdraw the word "obstruction".
The Minister of Finance has now been kind enough to supply me with a copy of the Appropriation Act of last year which says that the supplementary estimate covering this item last year was $198,010.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I thank the Minister of Finance for that information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Can the minister tell us whether this is expected to be a continuing item and what requests are coming in now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Certainly this is expected to be a continuing item. However there is no means of telling what the number may be in any one year; it varies a great deal from year to year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The minister says applications are coming in regularly. Am I not correct in saying that he anticipated on his main estimates that there would be a curtailment of assistance from the federal government in connection with this cold storage?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: What I actually said was that we had put a limit of $50,000 as the maximum amount of assistance available in respect to one of these cold storage plants, and that automatically cuts down the number of applications. Some of the big commercial concerns which were building cold storage plants costing $1 million and upward cannot now obtain a subsidy from the government amounting to more than the figure I have mentioned, and therefore the people who were chiefly taking advantage of this are in a different position.

Item agreed to.
Dairy products division-
501.	Grants and other assistance in accordance with the Cheese and Cheese Factory Improvement Act-further amount required, $143,327.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Shall item 501 carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Carried.

Supply-Agriculture

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No. Mr. Chairman, these are being called so quickly that one hardly has a chance-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Be fair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are saying "be fair" but surely we should have the opportunity to discuss the use of these moneys which are being asked for by the government.
This is an important vote amounting to $143,000. Can the minister give us any information as to who are receiving these grants in accordance with this particular arrangement?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Yes, I shall be glad to do that. The first of these is the Green Valley Cheese factory of Ontario, $4,620; the next is Fernand Sabourin of Hammond, Ontario, $49,450; the next is the Agricultural Society of Normandin, of Normandin, Quebec, $60,000; and the last is the Pine River Cheese and Butter Co-operative of Ripley, Ontario, $29,257.

Item agreed to.
504. Contributions to the governments of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the Minister of Agriculture, of one half the amounts paid by the governments of those provinces in respect of the transport of fodder, straw and other livestock bedding and the movement of cattle to feed from the 12th day of October, 1959, to the 30th day of April, 1960, $261,500.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: This is the contribution to the governments of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in connection with half of the amounts paid by the government to those provinces with respect to the transport of fodder, straw and other livestock bedding and the movement of cattle to feed from October 12, 1959 to April 30, 1960. Would the minister care to give us an explanation at this late hour of the night?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
An amount of $300,000 was voted in the supplementary estimates of 195960 to provide for these payments to the three prairie provinces concerned in accordance with the agreements which had been made to assist in the transport of fodder, under the adverse weather conditions and in view of the shortage of feed which prevailed. As it happens, the provinces were very slow in getting in their claims. No item was put in
the main estimates for 1960-61 but up to the time that the vote ran out they had put in for only $58,355 of the $300,000 which had been provided. So this is in effect a revote of that money so that the claim can now be paid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Do I understand that the $300,000 was the limit under the original estimate?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: We made an estimate that it would be $300,000, but the claims which have now been put in amount to somewhat more than that. The actual claims which have now come in and which remain to be paid amount to $261,500 and there was $58,355 put out on the other vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Is it expected there will be more claims, or are these the final claims?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: These are the final claims. This will close the thing up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: This is the last item under agriculture. Won't you let it pass?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
It being eleven o'clock I will rise and report progress.
Resolutions adopted this day in committee of supply reported and concurred in.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I should like to ask the leader of the house if he would be good enough to indicate the order of business before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Business will be taken in this order: continuation of the estimates of' the Department of Trade and Commerce, followed by those of the national research council, followed by those of the atomic energy board. The general program of the two latter organizations was considered in the committee on research which met earlier in the-session. Then after those items are finished the house will have left before it only the estimates of the Department of Finance and of privy council, one supplementary estimate-in agriculture and one supplementary estimate in external affairs. That is the only business before us now.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned,, without question put, pursuant to special order.
